heading: Linelist data / Datos individualizados
proposition: The Spanish bullet names the column as code-formatted `age` for the `age_group = ` argument, while the English says only "the name of the categorical age column" and the chunk beside it passes `age_group = "age_cat5"`.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader takes `age` to be the column to pass and writes `age_group = "age"`; `age` is the numeric age column in linelist, not a categorical one, so `age_pyramid()` produces an unusable pyramid with one band per distinct age or errors, instead of the 5-year bands the chunk shows.

heading: Load packages / Cargar paquetes
proposition: The English states that `library()` comes from base R; the Spanish drops the package name and leaves "con `library()` de **.**".
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader is not told where `library()` comes from, so the contrast the sentence is making (pacman's `p_load()` versus base R's `library()`) is lost, and the empty bold "**.**" reads as a missing package name they may go looking for.

heading: Compare to baseline / Comparer à une référence
proposition: The French text calls the case-data layer of the baseline-comparison plot a histogram ("Un histogramme des données de cas"), while the English calls it a bar graph and the chunk that follows draws both layers with geom_col().
reader_consequence: A French reader expects geom_histogram() for the case layer and may look for a numeric age variable or a binning argument; the chunk at chapters/age_pyramid.fr.qmd:473-541 uses geom_col() on the categorical age_cat5 column for both layers, so the described geometry does not exist in the code.

heading: Likert scale / Échelle de Likert
proposition: The French text names the respondent-classification column as `statut`, but the code chunks were not translated and use the column name `status`.
reader_consequence: A French reader looking for a column called `statut` in likert_data finds none; every downstream chunk (fct_relevel(status, ...), count(status, Question), aes(x = status)) refers to `status`, so the prose and the runnable code disagree on the identifier.

heading: #### Proportions, colors, & aesthetics / 割合、色、見た目
proposition: The translation states that the default dashed line inside each age group shows the median (中央値); the English says only that a dashed mid-point line is shown for each group, and the argument that controls it is show_midpoint, which marks a bar midpoint, not a statistical median.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes the dashed line to be the median of the age distribution in each group and may read, report or reproduce it as a statistical summary of the data rather than a plot-geometry midpoint marker.

heading: ### Compare to baseline / ベースラインとの比較
proposition: The English gives the reason for storing the maximum and minimum percent values: so that no bar is cut short. The translation states only that the values define the extent of the plot.
reader_consequence: The reader loses the link back to the red DANGER warning at line 293 about bars disappearing or being truncated when axis limits are too small, so they may skip computing limits from the data when adapting the code to their own dataset.

heading: ### Constructing the plot / プロットの作成
proposition: The translation points the reader to the warning ABOVE (前述の警告); the English text says the errors are discussed in the warning BELOW.
reader_consequence: The two files disagree on where the warning sits, so a reader comparing versions, or an editor syncing them, cannot tell which direction is authoritative; the English direction is in fact wrong, since the warning is at line 293, above this list.

heading: ### Compare to baseline / ベースラインとの比較
proposition: The translation describes the fourth shared column as the proportion of CASES out of the total (全体に対する発症数の割合); the English says 'percent of total', which in pop_data is percent of the population, not of cases.
reader_consequence: A reader may believe the percent column of pop_data holds a case proportion, and so misread the wide grey baseline bars in the final plot as case percentages rather than population percentages.

heading: ### Linelist data / ラインリストのデータ
proposition: The translation adds a parenthetical definition of a facet: 'a subset extracted for the factor value of interest' (注目する因子型の値を部分集合として抽出したもの). The English defines nothing here.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader is given a definition the handbook does not otherwise commit to at this point, so the term is anchored to wording that may not match how facet is defined in other Japanese chapters.

heading: Constructing the plot / Construindo o gráfico
proposition: English tells the reader to PREVENT bars from disappearing BY MAKING the count-axis limits auto-adjust to the data ('Prevent it by having your count-axis limits auto-adjust to your data'); the Portuguese says the opposite, 'Evite que os limites do eixo de contagem se ajustem automaticamente aos seus dados' = prevent the count-axis limits FROM auto-adjusting to your data.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is told to avoid the exact remedy the English recommends, so they keep hard-coded axis limits. On routinely updated data a bar that exceeds the fixed limit then vanishes or is silently truncated, which is the failure the DANGER box exists to prevent.

heading: Likert scale / Escala de Likert
proposition: The prose states the table below shows the Likert survey data, with a `status` column and 8 questions on a 4-point scale; in English the chunk beside it renders `DT::datatable(likert_data, ...)`, but in Portuguese the chunk renders `DT::datatable(head(linelist, 10), ...)`, i.e. the Ebola case linelist.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader sees the Ebola linelist (case_id, dates, age, gender) where the text promises respondent status and Q1-Q8 Likert responses. They cannot check the input shape for the whole Likert section and may conclude they imported the wrong dataset or that `likert_data` has linelist columns.

heading: apyramid package / Pacote apyramid - Linelist data
proposition: The prose names the argument to add as `proporcional = VERDADEIRO`; the code chunk immediately beside it (and the apyramid API) uses `proportional = TRUE`.
reader_consequence: A reader who copies the argument from the sentence writes `proporcional = VERDADEIRO` and gets an R error (unused argument / object 'VERDADEIRO' not found), because neither the argument name nor the logical literal is translatable in R.

heading: apyramid package / Pacote apyramid
proposition: English says the package help page is opened by entering `?age_pyramid`; Portuguese says to enter `?Age_pyramid` with a capital A, which is not the name of the function or of any help topic.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader types `?Age_pyramid` and R answers 'No documentation for Age_pyramid', so they do not reach the help page the sentence points them to.

heading: Aggregated data / Dados agregados
proposition: The display chunk that follows the `pivot_longer()` step is labelled as showing the aggregated data ('Visualize os dados agregados'); in English it renders `DT::datatable(demo_agg_long, ...)`, but in Portuguese it renders `DT::datatable(head(linelist, 5), ...)`.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader never sees the long-format table (age_cat5, gender, counts) that the next `age_pyramid(count = "counts")` call depends on, and instead sees the raw linelist, so they cannot verify what `pivot_longer()` produced or why `count = "counts"` is the right argument.

heading: Cleaning / Вычистка
proposition: The English says the intended age-category order is set by converting the column to class factor; the Russian says it is set by converting to 'коэффициент класса' (a class coefficient), which is not an R data type and not what the English states.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is not told to convert the age-category column with factor(), so they cannot follow the instruction and their pyramid keeps the default alpha-numeric ordering (e.g. '10-14' before '5-9'). The correct term 'Фактор' is used later at line 230, so the reader also sees two different names for one concept.

heading: Likert scale / Шкала Лайкерта
proposition: The English says `..count..` is used to invert the values TO negative (multiply by -1); the Russian says `..count..` is used 'для инвертирования отрицательных значений' (for inverting the negative values), which reverses the direction and is contradicted by the chunk at lines 665-673 where positive counts are multiplied by -1.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader reads the technique backwards: they understand the term to act on values that are already negative, rather than to make positive counts negative. That misreading breaks the one mechanism the whole pyramid/Likert construction depends on, and it is the mechanism this paragraph exists to explain.

heading: Likert scale / Шкала Лайкерта
proposition: The English data-management step says to pivot the data LONGER; the Russian says only 'Поворот данных' (pivot the data), omitting the direction.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader planning the step from this checklist does not know which direction to pivot, and must infer it from `pivot_longer()` in the chunk at lines 631-635. The same chapter translates the direction elsewhere (line 203), so its absence here reads as a deliberate difference.

heading: Demographic pyramids and Likert-scales
proposition: The five-point Likert example scale contains "Disagree" as its fourth option; the Turkish list gives "Katılıyorum" (Agree) twice and never gives "Katılmıyorum" (Disagree).
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader sees a five-point scale with a duplicated "Agree" and no "Disagree", so the worked example of a Likert scale is internally inconsistent and cannot be used as a model for coding response categories.

heading: **apyramid** package / Linelist data
proposition: The grey background bars show the range of the un-faceted data for that age group; the Turkish text instead says the grey bars show the range of un-faceted data "such as age group" ("yaş grubu gibi yönlü olmayan verilerin aralığını"), making age group an example of un-faceted data rather than the grouping the range is computed within.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader misreads what the grey background bars represent and cannot tell that each grey bar is the total for that age group across all facets.

heading: **apyramid** package / Missing values
proposition: Rows with NA in split_by or age_group do not trigger the FACETING described in the previous section; the Turkish text says instead that such rows "do not affect the formation of the graph" ("grafiğin oluşmasını etkilemez").
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the link to the faceting rule just above (NA is not counted as a third split_by value) and is told a broader, false claim that missing rows have no effect on the plot at all, which is contradicted two sentences later by na.rm = FALSE.

heading: **apyramid** package / Missing values
proposition: With na.rm = FALSE the missing rows appear in TWO distinct places: in an adjacent bar plot, and as a separate age group at the top of the pyramid; the Turkish text collapses this into one place, "at the top, in a separate adjacent bar chart".
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader does not expect a new age-category row at the top of the pyramid and may read that extra category as a data error rather than as the missing-age group.

heading: `ggplot()`
proposition: After the axis flip the two bar plots stand vertically with their bases meeting in the middle of the plot; the Turkish sentence omits that the bases meet in the plot middle.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is not told why one series is negated, so the geometric reason the two histograms join at zero to form the pyramid is missing from the method overview.

heading: **apyramid** package > Linelist data
proposition: The grey background bars in a faceted apyramid plot show the range of the un-faceted (whole) data for that age group; the Vietnamese says they show the range of the data that is absent/not present for that age group ("phạm vi của dữ liệu không có mặt cho nhóm tuổi đó").
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader reads the grey background bars as missing or excluded records for each age group, instead of as the total pooled distribution used for comparison across facets, and so misinterprets every faceted pyramid produced by split_by with more than two values.

heading: `ggplot()` > So sánh với đường cơ sở (Compare to baseline)
proposition: The Vietnamese file states the baseline-layer explanation twice: once as the untranslated English source paragraph at line 390, then again as its Vietnamese translation at line 392; the English has this paragraph only once.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader meets an untranslated English paragraph followed by its duplicate in Vietnamese, and may look for a difference in content between the two paragraphs that does not exist.

heading: ### Keyboard shortcuts
proposition: The keyboard shortcut that inserts the assignment operator `<-` is Alt + - (Windows/Linux) and Option + - (Mac); the translation gives Alt + * and Opcion + *.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader presses Alt + asterisk, nothing is inserted, and they conclude the shortcut does not exist in their RStudio or keyboard layout instead of pressing Alt + hyphen.

heading: ### Object classes
proposition: The base R function that converts to Date class is spelled `as.Date()` with a capital D; the translated conversion table names it `as.date()`.
reader_consequence: A reader copying `as.date()` from the table gets `could not find function "as.date"`, on a page that has not yet taught that R is case-sensitive in function names.

heading: ### Access/index with brackets (`[ ]`)
proposition: The first named element of the demo list defined in the adjacent chunk is `hospitals` (plural); the translated bullet describing that list calls the element `hospital` (singular).
reader_consequence: A reader following the bullet indexes with `my_list[["hospital"]]`, gets NULL, and cannot reconcile it with the very next chunk which uses `my_list[["hospitals"]]`.

heading: ### Functions with multiple arguments
proposition: The optional argument named in the adjacent `age_pyramid()` chunk is `proportional = TRUE`; the translated NOTE box names the argument `proporcional = TRUE`.
reader_consequence: A reader typing `proporcional = TRUE` gets an unused-argument error, and the note is the only place in the section that explains that fully named arguments can be given in any order.

heading: ### Delete packages
proposition: The English attributes `remove.packages()` to base R; the translation attributes it to the **utils** package.
reader_consequence: A reader is told a different package owns `remove.packages()` than every other language edition states, and may look for or try to load **utils** before deleting a package.

heading: ### Object structure
proposition: The example stand-alone vector of plot colours is `c("blue", "red2", "orange", "grey")`, which are R colour names; the translation gives `c("azul", "rojo2", "naranja", "gris")`, which R does not recognise as colours.
reader_consequence: A reader who reuses the example in a plot palette gets `invalid color name 'azul'`, and may conclude R accepts colour names in the session language.

heading: #### Scientific notation
proposition: The `?options` documentation says fixed notation is preferred unless it is more than `scipen` digits WIDER than scientific notation; the translation says fixed notation is preferred unless it HAS more digits than `scipen`.
reader_consequence: A reader believes `scipen` is an absolute digit count of the number itself rather than a width penalty relative to scientific notation, so they cannot predict when a value will print in exponential form.

heading: ### **Pipes**
proposition: The translated Pipes subsection opens with a second copy of the two-approaches list (Pipes/tidyverse versus intermediate objects) plus a new bold **Pipes** sub-label, content the English has only once in the parent Piping section.
reader_consequence: A reader meets the same numbered list twice within twelve lines and may look for a distinction between the two lists that does not exist.

heading: ### Languages other than English
proposition: The translation lists a third learning resource, [R for Data Science en espanol](https://es.r4ds.hadley.nz/), that the English list of non-English resources does not contain.
reader_consequence: None harmful: the reader gets an extra resource, but the Spanish and English editions no longer offer the same resource list, so a reader cross-checking editions sees content that is not in the source.

heading: #### Your library
proposition: The translation adds the condition "si es windows" (if it is Windows) to the instruction to look for a folder called "win-library"; the English states the instruction unconditionally.
reader_consequence: None harmful, and arguably clearer, but it is a claim about platform scope that the English does not make at this point.

heading: RStudio
proposition: In English, 'RStudio {#rstudio}' is a level-2 top-level section; in French the same section is written as a level-3 heading '### RStudio {#rstudio}', so it becomes a subsection of Installation and sits at the same level as its own child '### Orientation de RStudio'.
reader_consequence: A French reader sees RStudio nested inside Installation in the table of contents and in the section numbering, and cannot tell that 'Orientation de RStudio', 'Parametres RStudio' and 'Raccourcis clavier' are subsections of RStudio rather than siblings of it.

heading: Assignment operators / Operateurs d'affectation
proposition: The English says the assignment pipe is shorthand 'as shown below in two equivalent examples', then gives the pair 'linelist <- linelist %>% mutate(age_months = age_years * 12)' and 'linelist %<>% mutate(age_months = age_years * 12)' with the connecting sentence 'The above is equivalent to the below:'; the French sentence stops at 'Il s'agit d'un raccourci.' and no example, and no connecting sentence, follows.
reader_consequence: A French reader of the operators reference gets the claim that %<>% is shorthand with nothing showing what it is shorthand FOR, so they cannot see which normal assignment the pipe replaces without going back to the earlier Piping section.

heading: Statistical functions / Fonctions statistiques
proposition: The English gives the probs= example as the R vector c(0.5, 0.8, 0.85); the French gives it as c(0,5, 0,8, 0,85), whose elements are 0, 5, 0, 8, 0 and 85, so the stated example is not a vector of probabilities within 0 and 1 as the same sentence claims.
reader_consequence: A French reader who copies quantile(x, probs = c(0,5, 0,8, 0,85)) passes six values, four of them outside [0,1], and gets an error about probs outside [0,1] instead of the 50th, 80th and 85th percentiles.

heading: Object classes / Classes d'objets
proposition: The English lists the base R class-test functions as is.numeric(), is.character(), is.double(), is.factor(), is.integer(); the French list replaces is.factor() with 'is .facteur()', which is not a function that exists in base R.
reader_consequence: A French reader who runs is.facteur(linelist$gender) gets 'could not find function', and has no way from this page to learn the real name is.factor().

heading: Keyboard shortcuts / Raccourcis clavier
proposition: The English shortcut table gives the Mac shortcut for inserting <- as 'Option + -'; the French table cell for the same row contains only 'Option +', so the hyphen key of the shortcut is absent.
reader_consequence: A French Mac reader cannot learn the keystroke for inserting the assignment operator from this table, because the second key of the combination is not stated.

heading: Scientific notation / Notation scientifique
proposition: The English quotes ?options as saying fixed notation is preferred 'unless it is more than scipen digits wider'; the French drops the unit and says only 'a moins qu'elle ne soit plus large de plus de scipen'.
reader_consequence: A French reader does not learn that scipen is measured in digits of printed width, so they have no basis for choosing a value and cannot predict when fixed notation will be dropped.

heading: RStudio orientation / Orientation de RStudio
proposition: The French states the Git pane appears if you have linked the active directory to a repository on Github ('Si vous avez lie le repertoire actif a un depot sur Github'); the English only says the pane can be present 'if you choose to interface with Github' and names no condition about the working directory.
reader_consequence: A French reader concludes the Git pane depends specifically on the current working directory being linked to a Github repository, and may believe RStudio has no Git support for a project linked to a non-Github remote.

heading: How to install and load (Install from Github)
proposition: The English says the published CRAN version is the more stable one and the development version carries new features; the Japanese attributes both greater stability and the new features to the development version (より安定し、また、...新機能を備えた開発バージョン).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader concludes the GitHub development build is the safer choice and installs development versions by default, losing the stability trade-off the English states.

heading: Remove objects
proposition: English: rm(list = ls(all = TRUE)) clears the workspace (the R environment). Japanese: it 「作業ディレクトリを空にする」, that is, it empties the working directory.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader, who has just read a section defining 作業ディレクトリ as a folder on disk, may believe this command deletes files on disk: either avoiding it, or running it expecting files to be removed.

heading: R markdown
proposition: The English states R markdown documents are incredibly useful and versatile tools often used to create dynamic and automated reports; the Japanese paragraph omits this sentence.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn the main practical motivation for R markdown (automated, dynamic reporting) and may see it only as a way to produce one document.

heading: Object classes
proposition: The Japanese states the paste-percent-into-a-numeric-column example and the 'sometimes you must convert class' sentence twice, as two near-identical paragraphs (lines 1040 and 1042); the English states it once.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader reads the same paragraph twice and looks for a distinction between the two versions that does not exist.

heading: phantomjs
proposition: The Japanese calls phantomjs a package (パッケージ); the English calls it an external program, and the same Japanese paragraph later also calls it 外部プログラム.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader may look for phantomjs on CRAN or run install.packages("phantomjs") instead of webshot::install_phantomjs().

heading: Free online resources
proposition: The English quotation of the R4Epis mission covers common types of outbreaks AND population-based surveys; the Japanese quotation covers only 一般的なアウトブレイク調査 (outbreak investigations).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looking for survey tools concludes R4Epis covers outbreaks only and does not follow the link.

heading: Relational and logical operators
proposition: The English prose names the two case-definition variables hep_e_rdt and other_cases_in_hh, neither of which appears in the adjacent chunk; the Japanese names them rdt_result and other_cases_in_home, which do appear in it.
reader_consequence: The two versions disagree on the variable names of the same worked example, so a reader tracing the English names into the code chunk finds nothing to match.

heading: Code folding
proposition: The Japanese instructs the reader to leave a half-width space (半角スペースをあけて) between the header text and the four or more dashes, hashes or equals signs; the English gives no such step.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader treats the space as required syntax and may conclude a header written without it cannot fold.

heading: Object structure
proposition: The Japanese adds a translator note defining field epidemiology as the area that carries out infectious-disease epidemiological investigations (訳注: 感染症の疫学調査などを行う領域); the English has no gloss.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes an editorial definition of field epidemiology, narrower than the handbook's own scope, as part of the source text.

heading: Assignment operators
proposition: The Japanese adds a translator note explaining a parent R environment as the environment that sits above in a relation between several environments (訳注: 複数の環境の関係において上にくる環境); the English says only higher 'parent' R Environment.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader receives an explanation of environment scoping that the source does not make and that the linked base-R reference is not cited for.

heading: Mathematical functions
proposition: The Japanese function table adds translator notes distinguishing round() as 丸め（訳注: 四捨五入ではない） from janitor::round_half_up() as 丸め（訳注: 四捨五入）; the English table labels both rows simply 'rounding'.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader gets the round()/round_half_up() distinction from a bare table cell one section before the DANGER box that explains it, and may skip the explanation.

heading: Rounding
proposition: The Japanese adds a translator note defining banker's rounding as round-half-to-even (訳注: 最接近偶数への丸め); the English gives only the behavioural description.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader receives an added technical term that the source does not supply and cannot check it against the linked janitor vignette.

heading: Simple functions
proposition: The English says the summary() output is a summary of the column's numeric AND MISSING values; the Japanese says only 要約統計量 (summary statistics).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is not told that summary() also reports the count of missing values, which is why this example is applied to the age column.

heading: Statistical functions
proposition: The English example probability vector for quantile(probs =) is c(0.5, 0.8, 0.85); the Japanese gives c(0.5, 0.8, 0.05).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader copying the example requests an unsorted quantile set (0.5, 0.8, 0.05) and gets output that does not match what the English text illustrates.

heading: Function help / Auxílio para as funções
proposition: English tells the reader to get function documentation by searching the RStudio Help tab, by running `?thefunctionname` (function name after a question mark), and by searching online; the Portuguese section with the same heading omits all of this and instead repeats the `::` package-prefix explanation already given in the preceding 'Sintaxe do código' section.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looking up 'Auxílio para as funções' never learns the `?function` shortcut or that the Help pane documents functions, and reads a paragraph duplicated from the previous section instead.

heading: Pandoc
proposition: The Portuguese Pandoc paragraph opens with 'Sua versão de R é impressa no o Console R na inicialização. Você também pode executar o' before the Pandoc definition; the English Pandoc paragraph contains no statement about the R version being printed at start-up.
reader_consequence: The reader meets a sentence fragment about printing the R version spliced into the definition of Pandoc, so the sentence that should define Pandoc reads as broken and its subject is unclear.

heading: Languages other than English / Idiomas além do inglês
proposition: The Portuguese list adds a third resource, '[Ciência de Dados em R (Português)](https://livro.curso-r.com/index.html)'; the English list has only the Spanish and French resources.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is pointed at a resource the English handbook never vetted or listed, so the two versions no longer describe the same set of non-English resources.

heading: Access/index with brackets / Accessar-indexar com colchetes
proposition: The Portuguese chunk keeps the comment announcing the double-bracket example ('Apenas o segundo elemento, sem nome, usando colchetes duplos') but the code line `summary(linelist$age)[[2]]` that the comment describes has been deleted.
reader_consequence: The reader is told a double-bracket example follows, sees no such line and no output for it, and therefore cannot compare single- versus double-bracket indexing of a summary object.

heading: Access/index with brackets / Accessar-indexar com colchetes
proposition: The Portuguese comment says `summary(linelist$age)[2]` returns the second element 'sem nome' (without its name); the English says it returns it WITH the name, which is what single-bracket indexing of a named summary actually does.
reader_consequence: The reader concludes single and double brackets both strip the name, and so cannot see the distinction this example exists to teach.

heading: Access/index with brackets / Accessar-indexar com colchetes
proposition: The Portuguese states that single PARENTHESES ('parênteses simples') always return class list when indexing a list, and that 'os parênteses' can be written one after another; the English attributes both behaviours to square brackets `[ ]`, and parentheses do not index in R.
reader_consequence: A reader following the text may try `my_list(1)` instead of `my_list[1]`, which errors, and will not connect the paragraph to the bracket examples in the chunk below it.

heading: Object classes / Classe de objetos (Date row)
proposition: The Portuguese Date row says that once R is told data are dates the values 'só podem ser apresentados e manipulados de algumas maneiras especiais' (can ONLY be displayed and manipulated in certain special ways); the English states the opposite framing, that such data CAN be manipulated and displayed in special ways.
reader_consequence: The reader takes the Date class as a restriction on what can be done with the values rather than as the capability it unlocks, and may avoid converting columns to Date.

heading: Masked functions / Funções mascaradas
proposition: English introduces the numbered list with 'Here are ways you can fix masking:'; the Portuguese drops this sentence and starts straight at item 1, so the list is never stated to be the remedies for masking.
reader_consequence: The two numbered steps follow the masking screenshot with no introduction, so the reader may read them as a continuation of the diagnosis rather than as the fixes.

heading: Defining objects (`<-`)
proposition: The example cross-tabulation is of gender by outcome; the Russian text says the cross-tabulation is of gender by age (по полу и возрасту), while the chunk immediately below runs table(linelist$gender, linelist$outcome).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader expects age categories in the printed table, sees outcome values (Death/Recover) instead, and may conclude the code or the linelist is wrong rather than the text.

heading: Cheatsheets
proposition: The listed cheatsheet covers factors with the forcats package; the Russian renders it as Коэффициенты (coefficients), so it states forcats is about coefficients.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader learns the wrong purpose for forcats and will not look for it when they need to reorder or relabel a categorical variable; the same chapter later calls the class Факторы, so the two passages disagree.

heading: Object structure
proposition: A vector is a container for a sequence of singular (individual) objects; the Russian says последовательности уникальных объектов, asserting the elements are unique.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader can conclude that a vector, and therefore a data frame column, cannot hold repeated values, which contradicts every example in the chapter (e.g. c(1,2,3,4,5) usage, linelist$gender) and misleads them about duplicates.

heading: Missing values
proposition: The instruction that is.na() is the special function used to test whether a value is NA, and that it returns TRUE or FALSE, is stated in Russian nowhere: the sentence is left in English in the translated file.
reader_consequence: A reader who does not read English gets the code chunk with is.na(rdt_result) and no Russian statement of what the function does or what it returns, so the central point of the section is unavailable to them.

heading: RStudio orientation
proposition: The point that the Environment pane also holds a Connections pane for external connections and can hold a Git pane for Github is not made in Russian: the sentence is left in English in the translated file.
reader_consequence: A reader who does not read English does not learn that Connections and Git tabs live in that pane, and will not look there when setting up a database connection or version control.

heading: Why use R?
proposition: The English attributes the definition of R to the R project website (a third party); the Russian says на нашем веб-сайте проекта по R (on OUR R project website), claiming r-project.org belongs to the handbook.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader takes r-project.org to be a site run by the handbook authors, and so misjudges who defines and governs R and how authoritative the quoted definition is.

heading: R and RStudio
proposition: The English says to download the latest FREE Desktop version of RStudio; the Russian says only последнюю версию десктоп приложения and drops the word free.
reader_consequence: The download page offers free and paid Desktop editions; a Russian reader has no cue which one the handbook means and may believe RStudio Desktop must be purchased or may start a paid trial.

heading: Code assists
proposition: The English states the warning flag appears on the right side of the script; the Russian says only that RStudio places a flag on that line and omits where on the line it appears.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is not told which margin to look at for the syntax warning marker and may not notice it.

heading: Resources within RStudio
proposition: The English tells the reader not to include parentheses after `?functionname`; the Turkish tells the reader not to include an apostrophe ("Kesme isareti eklemeyin").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader keeps the parentheses and types `?filter()`, which does not open the Help page, while being warned about an apostrophe that the English never mentions.

heading: Twitter
proposition: The English sentence introducing the Twitter list ("R has a vibrant twitter community where you can learn tips, shortcuts, and news - follow these accounts") is present only inside an HTML comment in the Turkish file, so it is not rendered.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader meets a bare list of Twitter handles under the heading with no sentence saying what the accounts are for or that they should be followed.

heading: Cheatsheets
proposition: The English names the R package **leaflet**; the Turkish names a package **brosur** (the Turkish common noun for "brochure"), which is not an R package.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader searching CRAN or the RStudio cheatsheet page for "brosur" finds nothing and cannot locate the interactive-maps package. Every other package name in the same list (forcats, lubridate, stringr, purrr, dplyr, ggplot2, reticulate) is left in English, so the reader has no cue that this one was translated.

heading: RStudio orientation
proposition: The English says the Packages pane lets you see, install, update, delete, AND load/unload packages; the Turkish list omits load/unload.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn that packages can be loaded and unloaded from the Packages pane by ticking its checkbox, and looks only for a code route.

heading: Functions with multiple arguments
proposition: The Turkish instructs the reader to set `orantili = DOGRU` when the default is `YANLIS`, but the code chunk immediately below it (basics.tr.qmd lines 386-393) passes `proportional = TRUE`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who types `orantili = DOGRU` gets `unused argument` and `object 'DOGRU' not found` errors, because neither the argument name nor the logical value exists in R.

heading: Object classes
proposition: The Turkish class table states that a logical value must be one of the two special values DOGRU or YANLIS, and that these are not "DOGRU"/"YANLIS" in quotes; R's logical values are TRUE and FALSE.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader takes DOGRU/YANLIS to be literal R values and writes them in code, producing `object 'DOGRU' not found`; the quotation-mark warning also points at the wrong tokens.

heading: Missing values
proposition: The Turkish says `is.na()` returns "DOGRU" or "YANLIS"; `is.na()` returns TRUE or FALSE.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader compares the console output of `is.na(rdt_result)` (TRUE/FALSE, shown in the chunk at lines 1428-1431) against the DOGRU/YANLIS the text promised, and cannot tell whether the function behaved as documented.

heading: Statistical functions
proposition: The Turkish CAUTION box says missing values produce an output of "YOK"; the English says they produce `NA`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who runs `mean(linelist$age)` and sees `NA` does not connect it to the warning, and does not learn that `NA` is the signal to add `na.rm = TRUE`.

heading: How to install and load
proposition: The English says to force a re-install by using `p_load_current_gh()` WITH the argument `update = TRUE`; the Turkish says to use `p_load_current_gh()` INSTEAD OF ("yerine") the argument `update = TRUE`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader calls `p_load_current_gh()` without `update = TRUE`, so the forced re-install they were trying to trigger does not happen and the stale local version stays in place.

heading: Commenting
proposition: The English says you comment multiple lines by HIGHLIGHTING them and then pressing Ctrl+Shift+c; the Turkish says that pressing Ctrl+Shift+c comments multiple lines AND creates highlights ("vurgular olusturabilirsiniz"), turning the required first step into a result.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader presses Ctrl+Shift+c without selecting the lines first and comments only the single line the cursor is on, then expects some highlighting effect that RStudio never produces.

heading: Code folding
proposition: The English states that clicking the gutter arrow COLLAPSES the code down to the next header and puts a dual-arrow icon in its place; the Turkish sentence says only that you can click this arrow and the code below until the next header ends and a dual-arrow icon appears, and never states that the code collapses.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader is not told what the click actually does, so the following paragraph about expanding the code again (line 739) has no antecedent action to undo.

heading: Recommended approach
proposition: The English "Recommended approach" subsection recommends the R-project-oriented workflow built from three elements (an R Project for the files, the **here** package to locate files, the **rio** package to import/export); the Turkish file has no counterpart for this subsection at all.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader goes straight from "here is your working directory" to "do not use setwd()" with no statement of what to do instead, and never sees the R Project + here + rio combination or the cross-references to the R projects and Import-and-export pages.

heading: Set by command
proposition: The English subsection heading "### Set by command" has no heading in the Turkish file; its two paragraphs and DANGER box are merged into the parent "## Calisma dizini" section.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the section boundary and the table-of-contents entry, so the setwd() material reads as part of the chapter-level working-directory introduction instead of as the named alternative method.

heading: Set by command
proposition: The Turkish DANGER box tells the reader to use paths relative to the R Project root "with the **burada** package"; the package is named **here**, and the Turkish text elsewhere (lines 819 and 823) correctly writes **here**.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader tries to install or load a package called `burada`, which does not exist, and cannot follow the one recommendation the DANGER box makes.

heading: Defining objects (`<-`)
proposition: The English gives a reading mnemonic: think of `<-` as the words "is defined as". The Turkish states only that `<-` is called the assignment operator, and drops the mnemonic.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is not given the way to read an assignment line aloud, which is the point of the sentence, and gets a circular restatement of the heading instead.

heading: Relational and logical operators
proposition: The Turkish criteria table says the new `case_def` variable takes the values "Onaylanmis", "Muhtemel" and "Supheli" for tests on "Pozitif" and "Evet", but the `case_when()` chunk beside it (basics.tr.qmd lines 1396-1404) tests "Positive"/"Yes" and assigns "Confirmed"/"Probable"/"Suspected".
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader running the chunk gets English category labels that appear nowhere in the table explaining it, and may believe the code is filtering on Turkish strings that would in fact match nothing in the data.

heading: Statistical functions
proposition: The Turkish note names the `quantile()` argument as "prob ="; the English and the table directly above it (basics.tr.qmd line 1504, `quantile(x, probs)`) name it `probs =`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who writes `quantile(x, prob = c(0.5, 0.8))` relies on partial matching that the text never mentions, and gets an error as soon as the call is made in a context where partial matching is disabled or ambiguous.

heading: `%in%`
proposition: The English says: to ask whether a value is NOT `%in%` a vector, put an exclamation mark in front. The Turkish drops the negation and says: to ask whether a value IS in a vector, put an exclamation mark in front of the logical statement.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader adds `!` to test membership and gets the exact opposite result; the chunk below (lines 1556-1560) then prints FALSE for `!"a" %in% my_vector` even though "a" is in the vector, with no text explaining the reversal.

heading: `%in%`
proposition: The Turkish prose names the **dplyr** function "case_while()"; the chunk immediately below it (basics.tr.qmd lines 1564-1571) uses `case_when()`, and no `case_while()` exists in dplyr.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader searching the help for `case_while()` or typing it gets "could not find function", and cannot match the prose to the code example under it.

heading: Why use R?
proposition: The English says R-Ladies likely has a chapter NEAR YOU; the Turkish says it probably has a chapter that you are about to use ("kullanmak uzere oldugunuz bir bolumleri vardir").
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the actionable point (there is probably a local R-Ladies chapter to join) and reads an assertion about their own future use that the English never makes.

heading: Working directory in an R markdown
proposition: English: using R markdown inside an R project with the here package is much easier than the setwd()/root.dir approach just described. Vietnamese reverses the comparison, stating that setting root.dir is much easier than using R markdown inside an R project with the here package.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader concludes the handbook recommends hard-coding root.dir in the setup chunk over the R-project + here workflow, and adopts the brittle machine-specific path approach the chapter spends two sections warning against.

heading: Scientific notation
proposition: English: if the scipen option is set to a low number (e.g. 0), scientific notation is always turned on. Vietnamese instead says that if there are many small numbers to display (e.g. the number 0), the feature is turned on by default; it drops the fact that scipen's own value is what is set low.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader believes scientific notation is triggered by the data values rather than by the scipen option, so they do not learn that options(scipen=0) turns it on and cannot reason about why options(scipen=999) turns it off.

heading: Code assists
proposition: English: RStudio raises the warning flag on the RIGHT side of the script. Vietnamese states it appears on the LEFT side of the script.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader looks on the wrong edge of the editor for the syntax-error marker and concludes RStudio gave no warning about their missing comma or unclosed parenthesis.

heading: Assignment operators
proposition: English: the <<- operator defines an object in a higher 'parent' R environment. Vietnamese says it defines an object inside a function nested within another function.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader forms the wrong mental model of scoping: they think <<- is about nested function definitions rather than about writing to an enclosing/global environment, so they will misuse it and misread code that relies on it.

heading: Pipes
proposition: English says of %<>% only that 'It is shorthand'. Vietnamese states 'Nó nhanh hơn sử dụng pipe thông thường' - it is faster than using a normal pipe - a performance claim the English does not make. The chapter's own later passage on %<>% (vn line 1352) correctly renders the same English sentence as 'Đây là cách viết ngắn gọn' (this is a concise way of writing).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader believes %<>% executes faster than x <- x %>% ... and may choose it for speed rather than for brevity, and may expect a runtime benefit that does not exist.

heading: RStudio orientation
proposition: English states 'The Help pane can display documentation and help files.' The Vietnamese enumeration of the lower-right pane's tabs goes straight from the Viewer pane to the Files pane and omits the Help pane entirely.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is never told in the pane tour which pane shows documentation, so the later instructions to 'search the Help tab' and to run ?functionname and read the result 'in the Help pane' have no anchor in the interface description.

heading: Set manually
proposition: English states 'This will set the working directory for that specific R session.' The Vietnamese omits this sentence and jumps from the menu steps straight to the note about repeating it each time RStudio is opened.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is not told that the point-and-click setting is scoped to the current R session only, so they may assume it is a persistent RStudio preference and be surprised when file paths break in a new session.

heading: Code folding
proposition: English: one # marks a primary header, ## a secondary, ### a tertiary. Vietnamese writes '\# \# cho tiêu đề chính' - rendering as two hash symbols for the primary header - while still giving ## for secondary and ### for tertiary, which is internally contradictory.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader writing comment headers for code folding uses two hashes for a top-level header and gets a second-level entry in the script Table of Contents, with no top-level section at all.

heading: Free online resources
proposition: English asserts 'A definitive text is the R for Data Science book by Garrett Grolemund and Hadley Wickham.' The Vietnamese reduces this to a bare noun phrase naming the book and its authors, with no predicate and no claim about its standing.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader scanning a list of learning resources gets no signal that R for Data Science is the canonical reference rather than one link among several, and may not prioritise it.

heading: Import data / Importar datos
proposition: The translation carries a stray body line 'Importar datos' that duplicates the section heading; the English has no such line.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader sees the heading text repeated as a paragraph and may look for a separate sub-topic that does not exist.

heading: Split columns / Dividir columnas
proposition: The translation instructs the reader to supply 'en =' as the vector of new column names, but the argument of separate() shown in the adjacent chunk is 'into ='.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who copies the instruction writes separate(symptoms, en = c(...)) and gets an unused-argument error; the bullet list two lines below still refers to 'into', so the two names conflict.

heading: Change case / Cambiar mayusculas
proposition: The translation says the un-capitalised words are 'a', 'el' and 'de', but the string passed to tools::toTitleCase() in the adjacent chunk is English ('This is the US state of california'), where the un-capitalised words are 'the' and 'of'.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader looks for 'a', 'el', 'de' in the printed output, finds none of them, and cannot see what toTitleCase() actually leaves lowercase.

heading: Extract a match / Extraer una coincidencia
proposition: The translation states the search patterns are 'ensen', 'profesor' or 'tutor', but the chunk beside it searches the English pattern "teach|prof|tutor" over an English occupations vector.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader believes the example searches Spanish terms and cannot map the printed matches ('teach', 'prof', 'tutor') back to the described patterns; copying 'ensen|profesor|tutor' against the occupations vector returns no matches.

heading: Combine strings / Combiner des chaînes de caractères
proposition: The English states that `collapse = ` makes the output vector contain only ONE long character element; the French says only that the produced vector is "un long vecteur de type caractère" and drops the single-element point.
reader_consequence: A French reader does not learn that `collapse = ` reduces the result to a single string, so they may expect `str_c(x, y, collapse = ...)` to return one element per input pair and misread the printed output.

heading: Dynamic strings / Chaînes de caractères dynamiques
proposition: The French adds a description of the example data frame's contents ("comprenant la juridiction (zone), les nouvelles affaires et les affaires totales"); the English only says "Below is an example data frame."
reader_consequence: A French reader is told the column inventory in prose rather than reading it from the chunk, and the added gloss calls the case counts "affaires" (legal cases), which conflicts with the epidemiological meaning of `new_cases`/`total_cases` used everywhere else.

heading: Split columns / Séparer les colonnes
proposition: The English says of the `extra = "merge"` example that "no data is lost"; the French sentence omits that claim entirely.
reader_consequence: A French reader loses the explicit contrast with the following example (where third symptoms ARE lost), so the reason to prefer `extra = "merge"` is weaker and they may keep the default and silently truncate data.

heading: Wrap into paragraphs / Transformer en paragraphes
proposition: The English says that wrapping the command in `cat()` prints the output "displaying the new lines added"; the French says only that it prints the result "dans la console R" and omits that the inserted newlines become visible.
reader_consequence: A French reader does not learn WHY the second `cat()` example exists, so they may not realise that `str_wrap()` output shows literal `\n` until passed to `cat()`, and may believe `str_wrap()` failed.

heading: Detect a pattern / détecter un motif
proposition: The English states that the example search-term vector holds possible occupation terms for front-line medical providers; the French says only "les termes de recherche d'une occupation possible" and drops the front-line-medical-provider identification.
reader_consequence: A French reader does not know what the 45-term `occupation_med_frontline` vector is meant to capture, so they cannot judge whether the term list fits their own case definition before reusing it.

heading: Regex and special characters / Regex et caractères spéciaux
proposition: The English gives the alternative digit pattern as `"\\d{1,2}"` (escaped backslash); the French writes `"\d{1,2}"` with a single backslash.
reader_consequence: A French reader who copies `"\d{1,2}"` into R gets an "unrecognized escape" parse error, and the line also contradicts the metacharacter table earlier in the same French section, which correctly shows `"\\d"`.

heading: Split / séparer
proposition: The French says the value "fever" is located "dans le dataframe de l'exemple"; the English example involves only a single character string split by `str_split()`, with no data frame.
reader_consequence: A French reader may look for a data frame that does not exist in this example, and may conclude that `str_split()` bracket indexing addresses data-frame rows rather than list elements.

heading: Split columns / 列の分割
proposition: With extra = "drop", the third symptoms are lost (the excess values are discarded).
reader_consequence: The Japanese sentence states only that a warning is shown, so a reader who skims the prose and not the in-chunk comment can conclude the warning is cosmetic and keep the default, silently dropping every third symptom from the data.

heading: Extraia uma combinação / Extract a match
proposition: The text claims occupation 3 contains two matches of the search pattern; in the Portuguese chapter occupation 3 is "educador de escola primaria" and the pattern "educador|prof|tutor" matches it exactly once (verified with str_extract_all in R).
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is told to look for two matches in element 3 of the returned list, sees only one, and concludes that str_extract_all() does not in fact return all matches per string, which is the whole point of the section.

heading: Extraia uma combinação / Extract a match
proposition: The text claims that the second of occupation 3's matches is not shown by str_extract(); in the Portuguese chapter occupation 3 has no second match, so str_extract() and str_extract_all() give identical content for that element.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader has no worked contrast between str_extract() and str_extract_all(), and cannot see the first-match-only behaviour that the sentence asks them to observe.

heading: Substituir tudo / Replace all
proposition: The prose states the example replaces every instance of "morto" with "falecido", but the chunk immediately below it passes replacement = "obito", so the printed output contains "obito" and never "falecido".
reader_consequence: The reader looks for "falecido" in the output, does not find it, and cannot tell whether str_replace_all() misbehaved or the replacement argument means something other than the replacement string.

heading: Mudar maiusculas e minusculas / Change case
proposition: The prose claims tools::toTitleCase() leaves words like "para", "o" and "de" in lowercase, but the chunk beside it feeds Portuguese text and toTitleCase() only lowercases an English stop-word list: the actual output is "Este e o Estado Da Califórnia Dos EUA", with "da" and "dos" capitalised (verified by running R).
reader_consequence: The reader believes toTitleCase() understands Portuguese function words and uses it to title-case Portuguese place names, jurisdiction names or column labels, silently capitalising every "da", "do", "dos" and "de" in their output.

heading: Caracteres especiais / Special characters
proposition: The English table gives five separate rows mapping "\`" to grave accent, "\r" to carriage return, "\t" to tab, "\v" to vertical tab and "\b" to backspace; the Portuguese table collapses all five into a single mangled cell whose markup breaks the escape-to-meaning pairing.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader consulting the table cannot read which escape sequence produces which character for the last five entries, and the final entry renders as "\b"\ rather than "\b", so copying it into code produces an invalid escape.

heading: Caracteres especiais / Special characters
proposition: The Portuguese table defines backspace as "exclui caractere anterior ao selecionado" (deletes the character before the selected one); the English table gives only the bare term "backspace" with no definition.
reader_consequence: The reader takes an editing-key description of "\b" that the handbook never asserts, and may expect "\b" in an R string to delete a preceding character rather than emit a backspace control character.

heading: Split
proposition: The English points the reader to the R basics page as a navigable cross-reference, written as the markdown link [R basics](basics.qmd); the Russian writes the bare bracketed text [Основы R] with no link target, so the cross-reference does not exist.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who wants more detail on accessing list elements with [[1]][2] bracket syntax sees literal square brackets rendered as plain text, has no clickable route to the R basics chapter, and must find that chapter by hand or skip the background entirely.

heading: Replace by character position
proposition: The English states that the string "HIV" EXPANDS in length when str_sub(words, 3, 4) <- "XX" is assigned to it ("Note the expansion in length of \"HIV\""); the Russian says only "Обратите внимание на длину" (note the length of "HIV"), dropping the claim that the length grows.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told to look at the length of "HIV" but is not told what to look for, so they can miss that assignment via str_sub() lengthens a string shorter than the target positions (3-character "HIV" becomes 4-character "HIXX") rather than leaving it unchanged or truncating it. They may then assume str_sub() assignment always preserves string length and be surprised by longer output when applying it to a column of mixed-length codes.

heading: ### base R functions
proposition: The English says paste() is paste0() with a default sep = " "; the Turkish reverses it and says paste0() is paste() carrying the sep = " " argument.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader concludes paste0() inserts a space between parts. It does not: paste0() defaults to sep = "". Concatenations built with paste0() will silently lack the separator the reader expects, or the reader will use paste() thinking it joins with no separator.

heading: ### Detect within logic
proposition: The English names the dplyr function case_when(); the Turkish paragraph names case_while() three times, while the code chunk beside it uses case_when().
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader searching help for case_while() finds nothing, since no such dplyr function exists, and cannot connect the prose to the case_when() call in the chunk immediately below.

heading: ### Extract a match
proposition: The English says the third occupation contains two pattern matches; the Turkish says three patterns match within the occupations vector.
reader_consequence: The point of the example, that one single string can yield several matches inside one list element, is lost. The Turkish reader reads the output as three matched search terms instead of two matches within one string, and so misreads the str_extract_all() list structure and the following note that str_extract() drops the second match.

heading: ### Remove leading/trailing whitespace
proposition: The English gives the literal str_trim() side values "right", "left", "both" and the call str_trim(x, "right"); the Turkish translates them to "sag", "sol", "her ikisi" and writes the call as str_trim(x, "sag").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who copies str_trim(x, "sag") gets an error, because side must be one of "left", "right" or "both". The literal argument values a reader needs are absent from the Turkish page.

heading: ### Truncate
proposition: The English gives the literal str_trunc() side values "left", "right", "center"; the Turkish gives them as "sol", "sag", "merkez".
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who passes side = "merkez" to str_trunc() gets an error. The chunk beside the text uses "center", so the prose and the runnable code disagree on the only value the reader can actually use.

heading: ## Special characters
proposition: The English special-characters table says the escape "\`" represents a grave accent; the Turkish table says it represents the circumflex/caret sign ("sapka isareti").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader learns the wrong character for that escape and will look for a caret (^) rather than a backtick/grave accent when reading or writing escaped strings.

heading: ### Combine strings
proposition: The English says collapse = separates the elements of the output vector such that the output vector has only one long character element; the Turkish keeps only the first half, that it separates the elements of the output.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn that collapse = reduces the result to a single string. They may expect a vector with one element per person and be surprised when str_c() returns one long value, which is exactly the behaviour the example below demonstrates.

heading: ### Dynamic strings
proposition: The English says single quotes inside the surrounding double quotes are used to display single quote characters (''); the Turkish says they are used to display the double quote character (").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader believes nesting single quotes inside str_glue("") prints a double quote. It prints a single quote, so an attempt to show " inside a glue string fails and the reader does not learn that \" is needed.

heading: ### Detect a pattern
proposition: The English says negate = TRUE is for when you want to know whether the pattern is NOT present; the Turkish says it is for when you want to know whether the pattern is present or not.
reader_consequence: The inversion that negate = TRUE performs is not stated in Turkish. A reader who wants a plain presence test may add negate = TRUE and get exactly the reversed logical vector, which silently inverts any filter or case_when() branch built on it.

heading: ### Split
proposition: The English links the R basics page for more detail on accessing elements, [R basics](basics.qmd); the Turkish keeps the label but drops the link target, leaving the literal text [R temelleri].
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader cannot navigate to the R basics page and instead sees unrendered bracket text. The cross-reference that explains [[ ]] bracket indexing, which the paragraph depends on, is unreachable.

heading: ### Detect a pattern
proposition: The English gives the base R syntax as gsub(pattern, replacement, strings_to_search, ignore.case = FALSE); the Turkish gives the second argument the name replace instead of replacement.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who writes the argument by name, gsub(pattern = ..., replace = ...), gets an error or silent partial matching failure, because the formal argument of gsub() is replacement.

heading: Dynamic strings / Chuỗi động
proposition: English: single quotes inside the surrounding double quotes are used to display SINGLE quote characters ('') in str_glue() output. Vietnamese: single quotes inside the double quotes are used to display the DOUBLE quote character (").
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader who wants a double quote inside a str_glue() string will write single quotes and get single quotes, not the double quotes the text promised; the cited example (format string '%d %b %Y') produces single quotes, contradicting the translated rule.

heading: Truncate / Cắt chuỗi ký tự
proposition: English states the ellipsis IS counted within the maximum length given to str_trunc(). The Vietnamese replaces this with 'dấu ba chấm được tính toán phụ thuộc vào độ dài' (the ellipsis is computed depending on the length), which does not state that the ellipsis consumes characters from the specified maximum.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader calling str_trunc(x, 10) expects 10 retained characters plus '...' and is surprised that only 7 characters survive, so they choose the wrong width when standardising code lengths.

heading: Special characters / Các ký tự đặc biệt
proposition: English gives nine separate table rows, each pairing one escape sequence with its meaning, including the five rows "\`"=grave accent, "\r"=carriage return, "\t"=tab, "\v"=vertical tab, "\b"=backspace. The Vietnamese table has only five rows: the last five English rows are collapsed into one broken row whose meaning column contains only 'backspace'.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader scanning the special-characters table cannot read off which meaning belongs to \r, \t, \v or \b, because the four pairings are run together inside one cell and only 'backspace' appears in the meaning column.

heading: Cleaning dictionary
proposition: match_df() can take a long time to run on a large dataset, and further detail is in the matchmaker package documentation reachable with ?match_df.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader running match_df() on a large linelist has no warning that the call may be slow, so a long-running cleaning step looks like a hang, and they are not told to consult ?match_df for the remaining arguments.

heading: Quantile breaks
proposition: The English defines "quantiles" as the value below which a proportion of values fall and then contrasts that with "quartiles"/"deciles" as groups of data; the Spanish renders both English terms as "cuartiles", so it asserts that a quartile is the value below which any proportion of values falls and that quantile() returns quartile break points.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader concludes that "cuartil" covers every quantile and loses the distinction the paragraph exists to make, so they read the 95th percentile as a quartile and expect quantile() to be restricted to quartiles instead of arbitrary probabilities.

heading: Complex logic
proposition: Writing a final catch-all case_when() statement is optional, and its purpose is to assign a value for all other scenarios not described by one of the previous lines.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader is told to place TRUE on the left side without being told why or that the step is optional, so they may treat the catch-all as a mandatory part of every case_when() call and not understand that it exists to cover rows no earlier criterion matched.

heading: `replace()`
proposition: The prose states the gender is changed to "Mujer", but the code chunk immediately below assigns the value "Female".
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader following the prose writes replace(gender, case_id == "2195", "Mujer") and introduces a value that does not match any other gender value in linelist, so later tabulations and recodes on gender split into an extra category.

heading: Cleaning dictionary
proposition: The link labelled as the online reference for the linelist package points to the linelist clean_data reference page; in the Spanish it points to the matchmaker intro vignette instead.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader clicking the "referencia en linea para el paquete linelist" link lands on the matchmaker vignette they were already given earlier in the same section, and never reaches the linelist clean_data documentation the sentence promises.

heading: ### `age_categories()`
proposition: English says age_categories() can also be applied to numeric variables that are not ages ('non-age numeric variables'); the French says it can be applied to 'variables non numeriques d'age' (non-numeric age variables), reversing which attribute is negated.
reader_consequence: A French reader concludes age_categories() accepts non-numeric input and may feed it a character or factor column, which fails, while missing the real point that the function works on any numeric column (lab values, delays), not just age.

heading: ### Filter out missing values
proposition: English says drop_na() with empty parentheses removes rows that have ANY missing value; the French says it removes rows with 'toutes les valeurs manquantes' (all values missing).
reader_consequence: A French reader believes a bare drop_na() only deletes fully empty rows, runs it on the linelist expecting to keep almost everything, and silently loses most of the dataset because nearly every row has at least one NA.

heading: ### Automatic cleaning
proposition: English lists the accepted values of janitor::clean_names(case = ) as "snake", "sentence", "title", "small_camel"; the French replaces the literal argument value "sentence" with "phrase", which janitor does not accept.
reader_consequence: A French reader who copies case = "phrase" gets an error from clean_names() and has no way from the text to learn that the valid keyword is "sentence".

heading: ### Labels (French only)
proposition: The French file has an extra heading '### Labels' with the sentence 'D'autres logiciels statistiques tels que SAS ont des labels de variables.'; the English has no such section, and the point is already made in the preceding section (English line 169, French line 176).
reader_consequence: A French reader meets a numbered stub section that repeats an earlier sentence and promises coverage of variable labels that never arrives, and the section numbering of the French chapter no longer matches the English one for cross-referencing.

heading: ### Review distribution
proposition: English attributes comma-as-decimal-separator import problems to 'your R locale settings'; the French attributes them to 'les parametres par defaut de R' (R's default settings).
reader_consequence: A French reader, who is the most likely to hit comma decimals, looks for a generic R default to change instead of inspecting the locale, and therefore does not find why a numeric column imported as character.

heading: Import
proposition: The English says to load the raw linelist in R with `appliedepidata::get_data(name = "case_linelists_linelist_raw")`; the Japanese instead tells the reader to download an .xlsx file from a GitHub raw URL, while the code chunk immediately below (jp lines 126 and 130) calls `appliedepidata::get_data()`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader downloads an .xlsx and has no `linelist_raw` object matching the chunk they are told to run; the chunk beside the prose uses a loader the prose never mentions, so the reader cannot reproduce the import step.

heading: Import
proposition: The English states that the raw Excel file is imported and saved as the data frame `linelist_raw`, and that the file is assumed to be in the working directory or R project root so no sub-folders appear in the file path; the Japanese has no counterpart sentence.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is not told the object name `linelist_raw` nor the working-directory assumption behind the file path, so a file kept in a sub-folder fails to import with no explanation.

heading: tidyselect helper functions
proposition: The Japanese lists `summary()` as one of the **dplyr** functions inside which tidyselect helpers work; the English lists `summarise()`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader tries tidyselect helpers inside base R's `summary()`, which is not a dplyr verb and does not accept them, and gets an error while believing the handbook endorsed it.

heading: `across()` functions
proposition: The English closes the section with a pointer to online resources on `across()`, linking the rationale written by dplyr's creator Hadley Wickham; the Japanese section ends at the `.names =` bullet with no such pointer.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader loses the only signposted route to the deeper background on why `across()` exists and how it replaced the scoped verbs.

heading: Cleaning dictionary
proposition: The Japanese names the R package **matchemaker**; the English names **matchmaker**, and the code chunks beside it (jp lines 100 and 1043) load and call `matchmaker`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who runs `p_load(matchemaker)` or searches for that package finds nothing, because no such package exists.

heading: Cleaning dictionary
proposition: The Japanese instructs the reader to pass the dictionary data frame to a `distionary = ` argument; the English says `dictionary = `, and the chunk beside it (jp line 1044) uses `dictionary = cleaning_dict`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who types the argument name from the prose gets an unused-argument error from `match_df()`.

heading: `cut()`
proposition: The Japanese twice names the `cut()` argument `include.latest = TRUE`; the English says `include.lowest = TRUE`, and the code chunks beside it (jp lines 1283, 1311 and 1370) all use `include.lowest = TRUE`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who copies the argument name from the prose gets an error or silently keeps 0-year-olds categorised as `NA`, the exact trap the paragraph is written to prevent.

heading: Row-wise calculations
proposition: The English states that the columns to be counted are specified inside `sum()` by name within a vector `c()`; the Japanese has no counterpart sentence.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is not told how the symptom columns are handed to `sum()`, so adapting the example to their own columns requires reverse-engineering the chunk.

heading: Row-wise calculations
proposition: The English points the reader to the dplyr online vignette on row-wise calculations (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/rowwise.html); the Japanese omits that pointer.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader has no route to the authoritative reference for `rowwise()`, the least intuitive function in the section.

heading: One-by-one
proposition: The Japanese gives the example classes a column may hold as factor, numeric and logical; the English gives character, numeric and logical.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes factor as the ordinary text class for `add_row()` and is surprised when adding a value to a factor column is rejected as an invalid factor level, an error the chapter treats separately.

heading: Deduplication
proposition: The Japanese asserts that rows identical to other rows were removed; the English states only conditionally that any rows that were removed would have been 100 percent duplicates, without claiming any were.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader believes the de-duplication step changed the data and does not check the before/after row counts, which the English sentence is written to make them check.

heading: Manual name cleaning
proposition: The English states that the re-naming is done with the `rename()` function from the **dplyr** package, as part of a pipe chain; the Japanese introduces `rename()` with no package attribution and no statement that it runs inside the pipe chain.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn which package supplies `rename()`, so when the function is not found they do not know that **dplyr** (or **tidyverse**) must be loaded.

heading: Complex logic
proposition: The Japanese says the right-hand side of the catch-all `TRUE` statement can take a character-class value such as "check me!" or "missing"; the English offers "check me!" or missing, that is `NA`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader concludes the catch-all must be a text string and never learns that `NA` (via `NA_character_`, as the DANGER box below explains) is the alternative for unmatched rows.

heading: Quantile breaks
proposition: The Japanese says `quantile()` is used to obtain quartiles (四分位数); the English says it is used to get quantile break points at any probabilities the user supplies.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes `quantile()` to be a four-group tool, which contradicts the worked example immediately below that uses it to build ten decile break points.

heading: Examine the data
proposition: The Japanese states that the second, larger outbreak occurred in 2014-2015; the English names only the earlier smaller outbreak as being from 2012-2013 and gives no date range for the later one.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader treats 2014-2015 as a stated fact of the dataset rather than something to read off the histogram, and may carry that boundary into filters the chapter never justifies.

heading: Complex logic ({#clean_case_when})
proposition: The English gives a second, fuller `case_when()` worked example that builds a `case_status` column from a case definition, assigning "Confirmed" when `ct_blood < 20`, "Suspect" when `!is.na(source) & fever == "yes"`, and "To investigate" via a final `TRUE ~` catch-all; the Portuguese has neither the introductory sentence nor the code chunk.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader never sees a worked example of the `TRUE ~` catch-all clause, of ordering criteria from most specific to most general, or of applying a case definition with `case_when()`. The paragraph immediately above still instructs them to place `TRUE` on the left-hand side, but no example in the chapter demonstrates it.

heading: `across()` column selection
proposition: The Portuguese prose says the columns selected are those whose name contains the string "data", but the code chunk immediately below it calls `across(.cols = contains("date"), ...)`, which matches the string "date".
reader_consequence: A reader who follows the prose and writes `contains("data")` against the `linelist` (whose columns are `date_onset`, `date_hospitalisation`, etc.) selects no columns at all, and `across()` silently transforms nothing.

heading: Row-wise calculations
proposition: The Portuguese bullet says `num_NA_dates` counts the columns whose name contains "data", but the code chunk beside it uses `c_across(contains("date"))`, i.e. the string "date".
reader_consequence: A reader adapting the example with `contains("data")` gets `num_NA_dates = 0` for every row, because no `linelist` column name contains "data", and will conclude there are no missing dates.

heading: Cleaning dictionary
proposition: The English states that a fourth dictionary column named `order` can be used to specify the factor order of the new values; the Portuguese omits this sentence, and the word `order` appears nowhere in the Portuguese chapter.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader believes the cleaning dictionary supports only three columns, and has no way to learn from this chapter that `match_df()` can set factor level order, so they will re-order factor levels by hand afterwards or ship unordered factors into their tables and plots.

heading: Complex logic ({#clean_case_when})
proposition: The English states the general rule that a data row meeting none of the criteria is assigned `NA`; the Portuguese paragraph ends at "escrever primeiro os critérios mais específicos, e por último os mais gerais" and drops that rule.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader is not told the default fall-through behaviour of `case_when()` as a general rule. Rows matching no criterion become `NA` silently, which is easy to mistake for genuinely missing source data. The point survives only as an inline comment in the code chunk above, tied to that one example.

heading: Complex filter
proposition: English: `!column %in% c("a","b","c")` evaluates to TRUE when the column value is NOT A MEMBER OF the vector. Russian states it evaluates to TRUE when the column value "is not a vector" (не является вектором), which is a type test, not a membership test.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader learns the wrong semantics for the `%in%` operator: they may believe `!x %in% c(...)` tests the class of the column rather than excluding the listed values, and so write or misread filter conditions that silently keep or drop the wrong rows.

heading: `cut()`
