proposition: English lists as a drawback of `cut()` that you MUST supply accurate labels yourself ("You must provide accurate labels yourself"). Russian renders it as a permission/option ("Вы можете сами задать точные подписи" = you can specify accurate labels yourself).
reader_consequence: The bullet list exists to justify why `age_categories()` was written to replace `cut()`. A Russian reader reads label-writing as an optional convenience rather than an obligation carrying risk, so they are less likely to hand-check labels against the breaks and may ship mislabelled age categories (the exact error the following 'Check your work!!!' paragraph warns about).

heading: Review
proposition: English states that "POSIXct" is a type of raw DATE class. Russian states it is a type of raw DATA class ("тип класса сырых данных"), dropping the fact that the class is a date class.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader scanning the `skim()` output does not learn that a POSIXct column is a date column, so they may not connect it to the later `across(.cols = where(is.POSIXct), .fns = as.Date)` conversion step and may leave date columns unconverted.

heading: ### Core functions
proposition: English says `filter()` keeps certain ROWS; the Turkish summary table says it keeps certain columns ("Belli sütunların tutulması").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader learns the core dplyr verb backwards and will reach for `filter()` when they need `select()`, then be confused when `filter()` drops rows instead of columns.

heading: ### Core functions
proposition: English says `distinct()` de-duplicates ROWS; the Turkish table says it removes duplicate columns ("Duplike sütunların uzaklaştırılması").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader expects `distinct()` to drop repeated columns, so the de-duplication section later in the same chapter (which reduces rows) contradicts the reference table they were taught from.

heading: ### Etiketler
proposition: The Turkish file has an extra section heading "### Etiketler" plus one sentence ("SAS gibi bazı diğer istatistiksel yazılımların değişken *etiketleri* vardır."); the English has no such section between the column-names note and "### Automatic cleaning".
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader gets a numbered/linked section that promises coverage of variable labels but contains one orphan sentence and no guidance, and the material it announces is already covered in the preceding section, so the reader looks for content that does not exist.

heading: ### Automatic cleaning / ### Otomatik Temizleme
proposition: English lists a `clean_names()` capability the Turkish bullet list omits: you can specify particular name replacements with the `replace = ` argument, e.g. `replace = c(onset = "date_of_onset")`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn that `clean_names()` can rename specific columns during standardisation, so they add a separate manual `rename()` step for something one argument would have done.

heading: ### "tidyselect" helper functions
proposition: The Turkish prose tells the reader to use `include()` to select columns whose name contains a string, while the code chunk immediately below it (cleaning.tr.qmd:386-390) calls `select(contains("date"))`.
reader_consequence: `include()` is not a tidyselect function; a Turkish reader who types it gets "could not find function" and cannot connect the prose to the `contains()` call in the chunk.

heading: ### "tidyselect" helper functions
proposition: The Turkish text names the helper functions `end_with()` and `start_with()`; the English (and the helper list earlier in the same Turkish section, cleaning.tr.qmd:361-363) names `ends_with()` and `starts_with()`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader typing `end_with()` or `start_with()` gets an error, and the misspelling contradicts the correct spelling given a few lines earlier in the same section.

heading: ### "tidyselect" helper functions
proposition: The Turkish prose says "Match() fonksiyonu, include() fonksiyonuna benzer", naming `Match()` and `include()`, while the code chunk below (cleaning.tr.qmd:395-400) calls `select(matches("onset|hosp|fev"))`.
reader_consequence: R is case-sensitive and neither `Match()` nor `include()` exists; the Turkish reader cannot map the sentence onto the `matches()` call it is supposed to explain.

heading: ### Complex logic / ### Karmaşık mantık
proposition: English states that a data row meeting none of the `case_when()` criteria is assigned `NA`; the Turkish paragraph ends at "write the most specific criteria first" and omits this.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn the default fall-through behaviour of `case_when()`, so unexpected `NA` values in a recoded column look like a bug rather than the documented default, and the following paragraph about a final `TRUE ~` catch-all loses its motivation.

heading: ### Complex logic / ### Karmaşık mantık
proposition: The Turkish DANGER box offers an option the English does not: "Eksik (NA) ya senaryoyu ele almadan bırakın" (either leave the scenario unhandled), presented as an alternative to using `NA_character_`, `NA_real_` or `as.Date(NA)`.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader may believe that simply omitting the case is an equally valid way to produce missing values, which sidesteps the class-consistency rule the box exists to teach.

heading: ### Cleaning dictionary / ### Sözlüğün temizlenmesi
proposition: English points the reader to the online reference for the linelist package (`clean_data`) for more detail; the Turkish keeps only the preceding sentence and drops that pointer entirely.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who wants more detail on dictionary-based cleaning has no onward reference and must search for it.

heading: ## Row-wise calculations / ## Satır tabanlı hesaplamalar
proposition: English restricts the new column `num_NA_dates` to the number of columns WHOSE NAME CONTAINS "date" for which `is.na()` is TRUE; the Turkish bullet says only "the number of columns for which is.na() evaluates to TRUE", dropping the name restriction.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader thinks the count covers every column in the row, so the value produced by the accompanying `c_across(contains("date"))` code will not match what the bullet led them to expect.

heading: ### Review distribution / ### Dağılımın gözden geçirilmesi
proposition: English gives "4,5" as the comma-decimal entry meaning four and one half years; the Turkish renders the example as “5” meaning four and a half years.
reader_consequence: The example no longer illustrates a comma decimal at all, so a Turkish reader cannot see what a comma-in-decimal value looks like and is told that the value 5 means 4.5 years.

heading: #### `ifelse()` and `if_else()` / #### `ifelse()` ve `if_else()`
proposition: The Turkish text names the recommended function `case_When()` (capital W) twice; the function is `case_when()`, as the English and the surrounding Turkish code chunks spell it.
reader_consequence: R is case-sensitive, so a Turkish reader who copies the recommended `case_When()` gets "could not find function \"case_When\"" at exactly the point the chapter tells them to switch to it.

heading: #### Add to pipe chain / #### Tünel zincirine ekleme
proposition: The Turkish file carries an untranslated internal reviewer note inside the separator comment ("AYNI SATIR KODLARI 8 KERE FALAN TEKRARLANMIŞ. ANLAM VEREMEDİM, SADELEŞTİRİLEBİLİR SONRAKİ VERSİYONLARDA-çağrı"); the English separator comment has no such text.
reader_consequence: No effect on the rendered page, but the Turkish source carries an unresolved editorial query about duplicated code that was never acted on, so anyone maintaining the translation inherits an open question with no owner.

heading: Load packages
proposition: The prose beside the chunk says it loads the packages required for the chapter's analyses, but the Vietnamese p_load() chunk drops the `matchmaker` package that the English chunk loads (English line 98) and that the chapter's own executed chunk later calls as matchmaker::match_df() (Vietnamese lines 1024-1031).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader who runs the setup chunk as instructed never installs or loads matchmaker, so the 'Từ điển làm sạch' (Cleaning dictionary) section fails with 'there is no package called matchmaker' and the reader has no way to see where the missing dependency came from.

heading: Core functions
proposition: The Vietnamese says the essential functions listed below are the essential functions IN THIS PACKAGE (tidyverse) ('Các hàm thiết yếu trong package này được liệt kê dưới đây'); the English says only that the essential R functions DEMONSTRATED IN THIS PAGE are listed below, and the table beside it attributes functions to janitor, base R, epikit, matchmaker and tibble as well as tidyverse packages.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader concludes clean_names(), age_categories(), match_df() and add_row() ship with tidyverse, and will not install janitor, epikit, matchmaker or tibble, nor look for their documentation in the right place.

heading: Deduplication
proposition: The English says distinct() removes rows that are 100% duplicates ('it removes rows that are 100% duplicates'); the Vietnamese says it removes 100% of the duplicate rows ('nó loại bỏ 100% các hàng trùng lặp'), which asserts complete de-duplication rather than removal of exact copies only.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader treats distinct() as full de-duplication of the linelist and stops there, leaving near-duplicate records (same patient entered twice with any differing cell) in the cleaned data, which is exactly the case the dedicated De-duplication chapter exists to handle.

heading: Standalone (select)
proposition: The English states the rule for standalone use: the first argument is the original data frame to be operated upon. The Vietnamese instead says 'đối số đầu tiên trong bộ dữ liệu gốc sẽ được tham chiếu' ('the first argument in the original dataset will be referenced'), which never states that the data frame itself must be supplied as the first argument.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader does not learn the rule that a standalone dplyr verb takes the data frame first, and writes select(case_id, contains("age")) without the data, getting an error; the same rule IS stated correctly for filter() at Vietnamese line 1609, so the two sections teach inconsistently.

heading: Local and remote repositories / Repositorios locales y remotos
proposition: To clone is to create a copy of a Git repository in another place.
reader_consequence: The Spanish section never defines 'clonar', yet the term is used as established vocabulary in this section and in every later setup section ('Clonar desde un repositorio de Github', 'forking es clonación'). A reader meets the word without its definition.

heading: Local and remote repositories / Repositorios locales y remotos
proposition: Cloning works in both directions: you can clone an online repository FROM Github down to your computer, or start from a local repository and clone it UP TO Github.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader is not told that cloning has two directions, so the later section 'Nuevo repositorio de Github a partir de un proyecto R existente' has no conceptual grounding.

heading: Local and remote repositories / Repositorios locales y remotos
proposition: Once a repository is cloned, the project files exist in two places.
reader_consequence: The Spanish section opens directly on a dangling bullet list ('- el repositorio LOCAL ...') with no sentence introducing what the two bullets enumerate, so the local/remote duality that the rest of the chapter depends on is never stated.

heading: What does it look like now? > In RStudio / ¿Qué aspecto tiene ahora? > En RStudio
proposition: The bullet list describes the buttons circled in the image above, listed from left to right, and those buttons are referenced later in the chapter.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader gets an unintroduced list of seven items with no statement that they map to the circled buttons in the screenshot in left-to-right order, so the list cannot be matched to the image.

heading: Start-up files / Archivos de inicio
proposition: The README, .gitignore and license files may be created when the repository is created or added later, and they normally live in the repository root folder.
reader_consequence: The paragraph is left in untranslated English in the Spanish file, so a Spanish-only reader does not learn that these files are optional at creation time and belong in the root folder.

heading: Amend a previous commit / Modificar una consolidación anterior
proposition: Think before modifying commits that are already public and shared with collaborators.
reader_consequence: The warning is left in untranslated English, so a Spanish-only reader may run 'git commit --amend' on already-pushed commits and rewrite history that collaborators have pulled.

heading: Get started: create a new repository / Empezar: crear un nuevo repositorio
proposition: The Spanish text names Github Desktop and Rstudio->Git as the graphical interfaces you can create a repository from; the English only says 'from an interface' with no examples.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader is given a specific, narrowed menu of interfaces at a point where the English deliberately stays general, and 'Rstudio->Git' is presented as a repository-creation route that this section never explains.

heading: I want to pull but I have local work / Quiero actualizarme pero tengo trabajo local
proposition: The final step of the first strategy is to PUSH everything online; the Spanish says 'consolidar todo en linea', and 'consolidar' is this chapter's own established translation of 'commit' (see the heading 'Consolidar los cambios (Commit)').
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader follows commit, fetch, pull, resolve, then commits again instead of pushing, and leaves the merged work only on the local repository.

heading: Delete your branch > In Github Desktop / Borrar tu rama > En Github Desktop
proposition: The English instructs the reader to CHECK OUT (switch to) the branch to be deleted; the Spanish says 'comprobar la rama' (check/verify the branch), which is not a switch action.
reader_consequence: Github Desktop's Branch > Delete deletes the branch that is currently checked out. A Spanish reader who only 'checks' the branch without switching to it deletes whichever branch is active, potentially the working branch they wanted to keep.

heading: Sample commands / Ejemplos de comandos
proposition: In the command table, <name> stands for a branch name, <commit_hash> stands for the hash ID of a specific commit, and <num> stands for a number.
reader_consequence: All three placeholder tokens are absent from the Spanish sentence, which reads 'En los comandos de abajo, representa un nombre de rama. representa el hash ID de un commit especifico. representa un numero.' The reader cannot tell which placeholder in the table below means which thing, while still being told not to type the < > symbols.

heading: Sample commands / Ejemplos de comandos
proposition: git switch is an alternative to git checkout that is being phased in to Git.
reader_consequence: The Spanish table row says only 'Una alternativa a git checkout'. The reader does not learn that git switch is the newer command being introduced into Git, so has no reason to prefer it.

heading: Process overview / Resumen del proceso
proposition: The schematic is described in English as being in the format of a two-way table; the Spanish states it is a 'tabla de dos x dos' (a 2x2 table), a specific dimension the English does not claim.
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader expects a four-cell 2x2 layout and may not recognise the referenced image (github_table.png), which is a two-way table with more than two rows and columns.

heading: Install Git / Installer Git
proposition: English states installing Git from git-scm.com is a mandatory first step ("You must first install Git"); the French states it as an option ("Vous pouvez d'abord installer Git").
reader_consequence: A French reader treats installing Git as optional, skips it, and then finds that RStudio and Github Desktop have no Git engine to drive, with no instruction telling them the install was required.

heading: Process overview / Aperçu du processus
proposition: English says step 5 merges the online working branch into the online "main" branch in order to transfer the changes; the French says the merge is done "afin de créer une nouvelle branche" (in order to create a new branch).
reader_consequence: A French reader is told the purpose of merging is to create a branch, which is false, and never learns that the merge is what moves their work into main.

heading: Process overview / Aperçu du processus
proposition: English says the branch formerly called "master" is now called "main"; the French says it is now called "principale" glossed as ("master"), giving "master" as the current name.
reader_consequence: A French reader concludes the current default branch name is still master, so they will not recognise or look for the "main" branch that Github creates by default and that the rest of the chapter refers to.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github / Tirez et poussez les modifications vers Github
proposition: English glosses "committed but not pushed" as "(i.e. are still local)"; the French glosses it as "(c'est-à-dire qu'elles sont toujours en cours de traitement)" — still being processed.
reader_consequence: A French reader loses the definition that unpushed commits exist only on their own machine, which is the exact fact that makes those commits easy to revert.

heading: In Rstudio (pull/push) / Dans Rstudio
proposition: English gives the command `git config --global user.email "..."`; the French translates the configuration key and gives `git config --global utilisateur.email "..."`.
reader_consequence: A French reader typing the command gets a Git error, because `utilisateur.email` is not a Git configuration key; the very next bullet keeps `user.name` untranslated, so they have no way to infer the correct key.

heading: In Github Desktop (delete branch) / Dans Github
proposition: English instructs the reader to check out (switch to) the branch to be deleted and then use Branch > Delete; the French instructs them to "vérifier" (check) that the branch appears in the Branch > Delete menu, and drops the checkout step.
reader_consequence: A French reader never switches to the target branch, and Github Desktop's Branch > Delete acts on the currently checked-out branch, so they delete the wrong branch.

heading: This sounds complicated, I am not a programmer / Cela semble compliqué, je ne suis pas un programmeur
proposition: English advises: if you are NOT on a project where collaborating through Git is a necessity, it is a good time to get confident with it solo. The French inserts a second negation ("un projet où la collaboration ... n'est pas une nécessité"), inverting the condition so the advice applies to readers who DO need Git collaboration.
reader_consequence: A French reader who works alone reads the advice as not addressed to them and postpones learning Git, which is the opposite of the recommendation.

heading: Install an interface (optional but recommended) / Installer une interface
proposition: English states you can use the console occasionally for an action your interface does not support; the French note omits this.
reader_consequence: A French reader who hits an action their client cannot perform does not learn that dropping to the console for that one action is a normal, supported option, and may believe they must switch clients.

heading: Install an interface (optional but recommended) / Installer une interface
proposition: English states you can also perform any number of actions online on Github itself; the French note omits this.
reader_consequence: A French reader does not learn that the Github website is itself a usable interface for Git actions, so they will not use it when their local client is unavailable.

heading: Vocabulary, concepts and basic functions / Vocabulaire, concepts et fonctions de base
proposition: English states that it is good to have the vocabulary and concepts in mind in order to build a mental model, and that they are needed when using interfaces anyway; the French sentence stops after "nous montrerons comment utiliser les interfaces".
reader_consequence: A French reader is given no reason to learn the vocabulary section that follows and may skip straight to the interface instructions, then meet untranslated terms (commit, stage, remote) with no mental model.

heading: Commits
proposition: English's staging example has two pieces of work — model specification in one script AND later a figure in another script; the French drops "and later on a figure in", leaving only a model in "un autre script".
reader_consequence: The French example no longer shows two distinct pieces of work, so the case for two separate commits collapses, and the parenthetical that follows refers to reverting "les changements sur la figure" — a figure the French text never mentioned.

heading: In Github Desktop (commit) / Dans le bureau de Github
proposition: English says you give the commit a name and OPTIONALLY a description; the French lists the description with no marker of optionality ("donnez un nom à la livraison, une description, puis cliquez").
reader_consequence: A French reader believes a description is required for every commit in Github Desktop and spends effort writing one, or hesitates to commit without it.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github / Tirez et poussez les modifications vers Github
proposition: English concludes the note with the recommendation to push only once you are done introducing the changes for the task you were working on; the French note ends at the parenthetical and omits this recommendation.
reader_consequence: A French reader gets the comparison of revert difficulty but not the actionable rule it supports, so they do not learn when to push.

heading: In Github: submitting pull requests / Dans Github : soumettre des demandes de pull
proposition: English says a pull request can be submitted from the website OR from Github Desktop; the French says "à partir du site Web ... ou à partir de Github", dropping "Desktop" so both alternatives name the same place.
reader_consequence: A French Github Desktop user does not learn they can open a pull request from the application and assumes they must go to the website.

heading: Vocabulary, concepts and basic functions
proposition: The English says learning Git requires remembering 'a bit of vocabulary'; the Japanese says you must memorise 'quite a large amount of terminology' (かなりの量の用語を覚えなければなりません).
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader is told the terminology burden is heavy where the English deliberately downplays it, which discourages beginners the section is written to reassure.

heading: Vocabulary, concepts and basic functions
proposition: The English links the interactive tutorial to learngitbranching.js.org; the Japanese links it to learnngitbranching.js.org (extra 'n').
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader clicking the interactive-tutorial link reaches a non-existent host and cannot reach the recommended Git tutorial.

heading: Create a new repository in Github
proposition: The English says a private repository makes you 'encounter some quotas' in advanced special circumstances; the Japanese says 'いくらかの課金が発生します' (some charges/billing will occur).
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader believes making a repository private causes monetary charges when using Github actions, and may avoid a private repository for sensitive data on a false cost belief.

heading: What does it look like now? / In RStudio
proposition: The English adds the parenthetical instruction to pull first so the main branch is up to date before branching off it; the Japanese keeps only 'ほとんどの場合、main ブランチからブランチを作成します'.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader branches from a stale local main branch without pulling first, and later hits avoidable merge conflicts against the remote main.

heading: What we learned
proposition: The Japanese inserts a translator note glossing cherry-pick as 'いいとこ取り' and stating that cherry-pick is one of git's commands; the English gives no definition of the term.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader receives a definition not present in and not vetted against the source text, so the two editions differ in what they assert about the term.

heading: Where to enter commands
proposition: The English Option 3 gives a second way to open Git Bash, 'or open Git Bash form your application list'; the Japanese keeps only the right-click 'Git Bash here' route.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who has no 'Git Bash here' right-click entry is not told Git Bash can also be started from the application list, and concludes Option 3 is unavailable.

heading: Sample commands
proposition: The English defines `git rebase <name>` as appending the current branch's commits onto the <name> branch; the Japanese says it '修正' (modifies/amends) the commits from the current branch to <name>.
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader takes rebase to be a commit-editing command rather than a re-application of commits onto another branch, and misjudges what running it does to branch history.

heading: Resources
proposition: The English Resources entry links the interactive tutorial to learngitbranching.js.org; the Japanese links it to learnngitbranching.js.org (extra 'n').
reader_consequence: The Japanese reader following the Resources link for learning Git commands reaches a non-existent host.

heading: ### Create a new repository in Github
proposition: A private repository runs into usage quotas in advanced circumstances such as Github actions.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese sentence reads 'you will encounter certain advanced special circumstances' with the quota consequence deleted, so a reader choosing 'private' is never warned that Github actions minutes are metered and can run out.

heading: ### In Github: submitting pull requests
proposition: In the screenshot that follows, the branch named 'forests' is the one selected to be merged into 'main'.
reader_consequence: The caption identifying what the screenshot shows is absent, so a Portuguese reader sees an unexplained image and cannot tell which drop-down selects the source branch and which selects the target.

heading: ## Commit changes
proposition: Saved but uncommitted file changes appear 'no Github' (on the Github website), rather than in Github Desktop as the English states.
reader_consequence: The chapter carefully separates Github (the website) from Github Desktop (the local app). A reader told that local changes show up on Github will look on github.com for work that has not been committed or pushed, find nothing, and conclude Git is not tracking the files.

heading: ## Pull and push changes up to Github
proposition: The pull-work-commit-push cycle is repeated for as long as you work on the repository.
reader_consequence: The English 'Rince and repeat while you are working on the repository' is dropped, so the section reads as a one-off sequence rather than a loop, and a reader may pull once at the start and push once at the end instead of cycling.

heading: #### In Github Desktop
proposition: To delete a branch in Github Desktop you must first check out (switch to) that branch; the translation says only to 'verificar' (check/verify) it.
reader_consequence: Branch > Delete in Github Desktop acts on the currently checked-out branch. A reader who merely 'checks' the branch without switching to it will delete whichever branch is active, most likely the one they are working in.

heading: ### Commits
proposition: Git's staging area is named 'area de teste' (test area) and staged changes are 'mudancas graduais' (gradual changes).
reader_consequence: This is the one paragraph that defines staging, and it names a concept Git does not have. A reader takes staging to be a testing step or an incremental-change feature, and the rest of the chapter, which uses 'preparar/preparadas' for stage, no longer connects to the definition.

heading: ### Clone from a Github repository
proposition: The next step will be illustrated with 'Rstudio desktop' and with 'Github', rather than with Rstudio and Github Desktop.
reader_consequence: The two subsections immediately below are titled 'No Rstudio' and 'No Github Desktop', so the sentence contradicts its own headings and points a reader at a non-existent 'Rstudio desktop' product and at the Github website instead of the Github Desktop app.

heading: Create a new branch > In Rstudio Git pane
proposition: English points the reader to the image ABOVE for the purple new-branch icon ('see image above'); the Russian points to the image BELOW ('см. рисунок ниже').
reader_consequence: A Russian reader looks at the next image (github_rstudio_branchs.png, the branch history view) for the purple new-branch icon, which is not shown there; the icon is in the annotated Git_console.png figure in an earlier section.

heading: Commit changes > Amend a previous commit
proposition: English: an 'UNDO' button appears just under the COMMIT button, and clicking UNDO reverts the commit. Russian: a 'COMMIT' button appears just under the 'UNDO' button, and clicking that button reverts the commit. The two buttons are swapped.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader looks under an UNDO button for a COMMIT button that does not exist there, and is told that clicking COMMIT reverts a commit; following the text they cannot undo the commit in Github Desktop and may create a second, unwanted commit instead.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github > In Github Desktop
proposition: English states the purpose of the button: click 'Fetch origin' IN ORDER TO CHECK whether there are new commits on the remote. Russian states a precondition: click 'Fetch origin' IF there are new commits on the remote.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader believes they must already know that remote commits exist before clicking, so they never press 'Fetch origin' to find out; they then miss the described transition of the button into a 'Pull' button and cannot push, since the same button serves both.

heading: Merge branch into Main > In Github: submitting pull requests
proposition: English says a single branch NAMED 'forests' has been selected to be merged into 'main'. Russian says a 'forest of branches' ("лес" ветвей) was selected for merging into the main branch, i.e. multiple branches rather than one named branch.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader looking at the screenshot expects a multi-branch selection and cannot map the text to the single source branch shown in the drop-down, and may believe a pull request can merge several branches at once.

heading: Merge branch into Main > Delete your branch
proposition: English says the branch was merged into master (the master BRANCH). Russian says the branch was merged into a 'master FILE' ("мастер файл").
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told branches merge into a file rather than into another branch, which contradicts the merge instructions given two sections earlier (git checkout master; git merge ...) and blurs the branch concept the chapter is teaching.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github
proposition: English concludes the note with 'it is better to PUSH when you are done with introducing changes on the task you were working on'; the Turkish concludes 'commit etmek daha iyidir' (it is better to COMMIT).
reader_consequence: The note's whole premise is that committed-but-unpushed changes are easy to revert while pushed ones are not, so the advice must be about timing the PUSH. A Turkish reader gets advice to delay committing instead, which contradicts the chapter's repeated instruction to commit often and small, and leaves them unsure when to push.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github > In Rstudio
proposition: English states that the RStudio 'Pull' icon (downward arrow) fetches and pulls at the same time; the Turkish says only to click the icon and drops 'which fetches and pulls at the same time'.
reader_consequence: The chapter elsewhere teaches fetch and pull as two distinct operations. A Turkish reader is not told that the one RStudio button performs both, so they may look for a separate fetch control in RStudio or believe they must fetch some other way before pulling.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github > In Rstudio
proposition: English says the linked tutorial chapters show how to connect to a repository using an SSH key, and warns it is 'more complicated'; the Turkish keeps only 'see chapters 10 and 11 of this tutorial to connect to a repository'.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader tired of typing a password is not told what the remedy actually is (an SSH key) nor that it is harder than the methods already shown, so they cannot judge whether to follow the link.

heading: Vocabulary, concepts and basic functions > Commits
proposition: English gives the reason for splitting the model-script and figure-script work into two commits: 'it would be easier in case you wanted to revert the changes on the figure but not the model'. The Turkish parenthesis is truncated to 'sekildeki degisiklikleri geri almak isteyip modeli' and never states the 'but not the model' contrast or the ease-of-reverting rationale.
reader_consequence: The example loses its point. A Turkish reader sees an instruction to make two commits with no reason, so they cannot generalise the rule (group changes so that any one group can be reverted alone) to their own work.

heading: What is Git?
proposition: English says Git works like the 'track change' option in Word, LibreOffice or Google docs 'but for all types of files'; the Turkish keeps the analogy and drops 'but for all types of files'.
reader_consequence: The clause is the point of the analogy: it tells the reader Git is not limited to text documents and tracks scripts, data files and images too. Without it a Turkish reader may assume Git only versions word-processor-like documents.

heading: Resources
proposition: English lists the resource URL https://tutorialzine.com/2016/06/learn-git-in-30-minutes; the Turkish gives https://tutorialzine.com/2016/06/learn-git-in-30-dakika, with the word 'minutes' inside the URL path translated to 'dakika'.
reader_consequence: The link is dead. A Turkish reader who clicks the recommended 'basic and advanced' tutorial gets a 404 and has no way to guess the correct address.

heading: Resources
proposition: English lists https://ohi-science.org/news/github-going-back-in-time; the Turkish lists https://ohi-science.org/news/github-coming-back-in-time ('going' changed to 'coming').
reader_consequence: The link is dead, so a Turkish reader loses the recommended article on reverting a Git repository to an earlier state.

heading: Setup > Install an interface (optional but recommended)
proposition: English states that the RStudio Git pane and Github Desktop are the two beginner interfaces 'which we will showcase in this chapter'; the Turkish renders this as 'ki bu bolumde durum nasil olacak', which does not state that the chapter demonstrates those two interfaces.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader is not told that the two named beginner tools are the ones the rest of the chapter walks through, so they may install one of the intermediate clients named in the next sentence and then find no matching instructions.

heading: What does it look like now? / In RStudio
proposition: The translation states the blue *pull* icon in the RStudio Git pane is an UPWARD-pointing arrow; the English states no direction, and in RStudio (and in the translation's own later text) the pull arrow points DOWN.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader looking at the circled buttons in the Git_console.png image identifies the wrong icon as pull, and will click push when intending to pull.

heading: What does it look like now? / In RStudio
proposition: The translation states the green *push* icon in the RStudio Git pane is a DOWNWARD-pointing arrow; the English states no direction, and the translation's own Rstudio pull/push section (line 424) says push is the upward arrow.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader identifies the wrong icon as push; the chapter also contradicts itself between line 232 and line 424, so the reader cannot resolve which is correct.

heading: Pull and push changes up to Github / In Github Desktop
proposition: The translation says that when Git finds new commits on the remote, the button changes into a "Push" button; the English says it changes into a "Pull" button (and the image beside it is github_desktop_pull_button.png).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader expects the wrong label in Github Desktop, and the very next clause (you cannot push before you pull) becomes self-contradictory, so the pull-before-push rule is lost.

heading: What we learned
proposition: The translation says fuller Git interfaces let you do more by point-and-click but "usually you must pay a fee"; the English says the cost is a more complex layout, not money.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader believes tools such as SourceTree or GitKraken require payment and rules them out, when the English only warns that their interface is more complex.

heading: What we learned
proposition: The translation adds a parenthetical definition of cherry-pick as "taking only a few commits from a PR"; the English gives no definition and does not tie cherry-picking to pull requests.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader learns a narrowed, PR-specific meaning of cherry-pick and may not recognise it as a general operation on any commit from any branch.

heading: Get started: create a new repository
proposition: The translation says a new repository can be created from the "R console"; the English says "the console", which throughout this chapter means the Git shell/terminal (the "In console" sections all show bash commands).
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader types git commands into the R console, where they fail, instead of using the RStudio Terminal or Git Bash.

heading: Branches
proposition: The English offers deleting the BRANCH when the experiment was unsuccessful; the translation instead says to delete the unsuccessful CHANGES, so the option of discarding the whole branch is not stated.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader does not learn that an abandoned branch can simply be deleted, and may try to undo edits file by file instead.

heading: This sounds complicated, I am not a programmer
proposition: The English concedes that Git can indeed be complicated ("It can be."); the translation instead asserts that the reader is fully able ("Ban hoan toan co the.").
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader loses the concession that sets up the following 'However, much like R or Excel...' contrast, so the paragraph's reassurance no longer answers the heading's worry.

heading: UpSetR
proposition: The French states that `+()` converts the 1s and 0s according to a logical statement ("qui convertit les 1 et les 0 en fonction d'une declaration logique"), whereas the English states that `+()` converts TO 1s and 0s based on a logical statement; the code beside it (`~+(.x == "yes")`) turns a logical test into 1/0 output, not the reverse.
reader_consequence: A French reader takes 1/0 values as the INPUT of `+()` rather than its output, so they may believe the yes/no to 1/0 recode must already have happened before `+()` is applied, and will misread the `across(..., .fns = ~+(.x == "yes"))` line in the chunk that follows.

heading: Combinations analysis / 複数回答データの分析
proposition: The English says the horizontal bars showing the frequency of each individual symptom are to the RIGHT of the plot; the Japanese says they are on the LEFT (左側の横棒).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looking for the per-symptom frequency bars is directed to the opposite side of the example plot from the side the English text names, so the two editions disagree about how to read the same figure and the reader may misidentify which bars are the set-size bars.

heading: Re-format values / 変数の値を変換する
proposition: The English tells the reader to note TWO new columns towards the right end of the data: the pasted combined character values (all_symptoms) and the list column (all_symptoms_list); the Japanese mentions only the single rightmost list column.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader inspecting the displayed table does not know to check the intermediate all_symptoms character column created by unite(), so they cannot verify the semicolon-concatenation step that the preceding code performed and may not understand why two columns exist.

heading: ggupset / **ggupset** パッケージでプロットを作成する
proposition: The English locates the offline package documentation in the RStudio Help tab (`?ggupset`); the Japanese instructs the reader to run `?ggupset` in the RStudio console.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader is given a different action from the English text for reaching the offline documentation, and is not told that the result appears in the RStudio Help pane, so they may not know where to look for the output.

heading: Combinations analysis / Análise de Combinações
proposition: The horizontal bars showing the frequency of each individual symptom are located to the RIGHT of the plot; the translation says they are to the LEFT ("À esquerda").
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looking at the UpSet figure is directed to the wrong side of the plot when trying to identify the per-symptom frequency bars, and may mistake the vertical combination bars or the intersection matrix for the individual-symptom totals.

heading: `UpSetR`
proposition: The English offers a more efficient alternative for the yes/no to 1/0 conversion, using the `+()` function together with `across()` to change several columns at once, and links to the [Cleaning data and core functions](cleaning.qmd#clean_across) page; the whole paragraph and its accompanying code chunk are absent from the translation.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader never learns the compact `across(..., .fns = ~+(.x == "yes"))` idiom nor the cross-reference to the data-cleaning chapter, so they are left with only the five repeated per-column recodes and miss a technique the handbook expects them to reuse elsewhere.

heading: UpSetR
proposition: The English points the reader to the Cleaning data and core functions chapter (link target cleaning.qmd#clean_across); the Russian link target is only the bare fragment #clean_across, so it no longer names that chapter.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who clicks the cross-reference for more on across() stays on the combination-analysis page instead of reaching the cleaning chapter section (cleaning.ru.qmd line 646), and so misses the fuller explanation of across().

heading: Re-format values / Değerleri yeniden biçimlendir
proposition: The English names the dplyr function `case_when()`; the Turkish names `case_while()`, which is not a function in dplyr or in base R.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who searches for or types `case_while()` gets 'could not find function' and cannot locate the documented approach, because no such function exists in any package.

heading: Re-format values / Değerleri yeniden biçimlendir
proposition: The English converts the "yes" and "no" values INTO the symptom name; the Turkish states the reverse, that the actual symptom name is converted INTO "evet" and "hayır" ("gerçek semptom adını 'evet' ve 'hayır'a dönüştürürüz").
reader_consequence: The reader is told the transformation runs in the opposite direction from what the code chunk below does (`ifelse(fever == "yes", "fever", NA)`), so the reader cannot reconcile the sentence with the code and may build the reverse recode, which produces no symptom labels for ggupset.

heading: UpSetR
proposition: The comment beside the recode says the "yes"/"no" values are converted into the symptom name itself ("semptom adının kendisine dönüştürün"), but the code beside it converts them to 1 and 0; the English comment correctly says "convert the "yes" and "no" values into 1s and 0s".
reader_consequence: The reader is told this UpSetR data-cleaning step produces symptom-name strings, when it produces the 1/0 indicator columns UpSetR requires, so the reader may think the ggupset recode is being repeated and skip or duplicate the step.

heading: Load packages / Paketleri yükleyin
proposition: The English points the reader to the R basics page with a working cross-reference, `[R basics](basics.qmd)`; the Turkish keeps only the bracketed label `[R basics]` with no link target.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader sees literal bracket text instead of a link and cannot reach the R basics page for the referenced background on R packages.

heading: Re-format values / Değerleri yeniden biçimlendir
proposition: The English links the Characters and strings page with a working cross-reference, `[Characters and strings](characters_strings.qmd)`; the Turkish keeps only the bracketed label `[Karakterler ve dizeler]` with no link target.

heading: UpSetR
proposition: The English links to another chapter for `across()`, `[Cleaning data and core functions](cleaning.qmd#clean_across)`; the Turkish drops the file part and leaves only the fragment `(#clean_across)`.
reader_consequence: The link resolves to an anchor on the combinations-analysis page itself, which has no `clean_across` anchor, so the Turkish reader clicking it stays put and never reaches the cleaning chapter's explanation of `across()`.

heading: Combinations analysis / Biểu đồ kết hợp
proposition: The horizontal bars showing the frequency of each individual symptom are located on the RIGHT of the UpSet plot; the Vietnamese says they are on the left ("Ở bên trái").
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader looking at the example UpSet plot searches the left-hand side for the per-symptom frequency bars, finds the set-size bars are not where the text says, and may mis-read the horizontal bars they do find (or the vertical combination bars) as the wrong quantity.

heading: `UpSetR`
proposition: The `+()` function converts values to 1s and 0s based on a logical statement.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader is shown `~+(.x == "yes")` with no explanation of what the leading `+` does, so they cannot tell that it is the operator performing the logical-to-numeric coercion, and cannot adapt the idiom to another condition or another dataset.

heading: `UpSetR`
proposition: The `across()` + `+()` command is offered as a MORE EFFICIENT alternative to the preceding per-column `case_when()`/`ifelse()` block ("If you are interested in a more efficient command").
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader sees the second chunk as an unmotivated extra example rather than a recommended shorter replacement for the five repeated per-column recodes, and keeps writing the long form.

heading: Follow-up data / Datos de seguimiento
proposition: The English states the total number of rows in the followups dataset (via the inline expression nrow(followups)) alongside the statement that only the first 50 rows are shown; the Spanish states only that the first 50 rows of followups are shown and gives no total.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader is not told how large the followups dataset is, so they cannot judge what fraction of the follow-up records the displayed 50-row table represents. proposition: The recommended visualisation for per-contact daily follow-up status is a heat plot; the French says it is a scatter plot ("diagramme de dispersion").
reader_consequence: A French reader is told the chunk below builds a scatter plot, while `geom_tile()` builds a heat plot. The reader learns the wrong name for the technique and cannot connect it to the linked heat-plot page, nor reach for `geom_tile()` when a heat plot is wanted.

heading: Transmission Matrices / Matrices de transmission
proposition: The chunk that follows creates a heat map of age-by-age transmission; the French says it creates a geographic map ("une carte géographique pour l'âge").
reader_consequence: A French reader expects a map of places from a chunk that plots age classes on both axes with `geom_tile()`. The reader misreads the whole transmission-matrix example and may look for absent geographic columns.

proposition: The follow-up day number is computed as the difference between the encounter date and the intended follow-up start date; the French says it is the difference between the date of the LAST encounter ("la date de la dernière rencontre") and that start date.
reader_consequence: A French reader building the missing follow-up-day column computes one value per contact from the last encounter, instead of one value per encounter row. The resulting column cannot drive the 1-14 x-axis of the heat plot below.

heading: Data cleaning / Nettoyage de données
proposition: Wide-format follow-up data commonly arrive as an Excel sheet; the French drops the Excel sheet entirely and says only "sous la forme d'une large".
reader_consequence: A French reader loses the concrete example of the format these data usually arrive in, and the sentence is left without a noun, so the wide-versus-long point is harder to recognise in their own Excel exports.

heading: Daily individual tracking
proposition: The Japanese states that the `followups` data has one column created for each follow-up day 1-14 (「1 ～ 14 日まで一日ごとに列が作成してあります」, and that a missing one must be built as 「1 ～ 14 日まで一日ごとに列を作成する」); the English states there is a single column holding the follow-up day number (1-14), and the adjacent code plots the single column `followup_number`.

heading: Daily individual tracking
proposition: The Japanese says the follow-up day number is computed as the difference between the exposure date (曝露日（調査対象の接触者が感染者と接触した日）) and the follow-up start date; the English says it is the difference between the encounter date (the date of the individual follow-up visit) and the date follow-up was intended to begin.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader computing exposure date minus follow-up start date gets one constant value per contact, not a 1-14 day counter that varies across that contact's visits, so the heat plot has a single tile column per contact instead of a follow-up timeline.

heading: Follow-up data
proposition: The Japanese says the table below shows the first `nrow(followups)` records of the follow-up data; the English says it shows the first 50 rows of the `nrow(followups)`-row dataset, and the chunk at lines 129-131 calls `head(followups, 50)`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader takes the displayed table to be the whole `followups` dataset rather than a 50-row preview, and loses the English statement of how many rows the dataset actually has.
