proposition: The Vietnamese says library() from base R installs a package ("cài đặt package với hàm library()"); the English says library() loads an already-installed package.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader believes library() will install a missing package, so runs library() on an uninstalled package, gets "there is no package called ...", and has no stated route to install it.

heading: Epicurves with ggplot2
proposition: The Vietnamese opens the sentence with "Unlike using the incidence2 package" ("Không giống như sử dụng package incidence2"), asserting a contrast with incidence2 behaviour that the English sentence does not make.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader infers that incidence2 handles time aggregation and date-axis labelling automatically, a claim the chapter never supports or demonstrates, and may choose incidence2 on that basis.

heading: Specify case bins
proposition: The Vietnamese says binwidth = is set to the number of bins of the histogram ("đặt binwidth = bằng số bins của histogram, tính bằng ngày"); the English says binwidth = sets the width of the histogram bins, in days.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader sets binwidth to the desired count of bars rather than the bar width in days, producing an epicurve with the wrong time aggregation while the code runs without error.

heading: Weekly epicurve example
proposition: The English bullet list states that closed = "left" is used in geom_histogram() to ensure dates are counted in the correct bins; the Vietnamese bullet list omits this point.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader building a weekly epicurve does not know to set closed = "left", so cases falling exactly on a Monday break are assigned to the previous week and every weekly count near a boundary can be off by those cases.

heading: Multi-level date labels
proposition: The English states that the easiest method for multi-level date labels is passing scales::label_date_short() to the labels = argument of scale_x_date(), and that its labels adapt automatically as the data span grows from days to weeks to months and years; the Vietnamese omits this paragraph and presents only the faceting method.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader never learns the simplest solution to the stated problem and instead implements the far more involved facet_grid() workaround, which also forces a geom_area() instead of a histogram.

heading: Cumulative Incidence
proposition: The Vietnamese adds a note that a reader using incidence2 should see the chapter section on computing cumulative incidence with a single simple function, and that this section covers the ggplot() route; the English has no such note.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader searches the chapter for an incidence2 cumulative-incidence function that is never named or shown, and may abandon the ggplot() method described here while looking for it.

heading: R Markdown errors / Errores de R Markdown
proposition: The English quotes the literal knitr diagnostic as `Error in options[[sprintf("fig.%s", i)]]`; the Spanish quotes it as `Error en options[sprintf("fig.%s", i)]]`, translating the English keyword "in" to "en" and reducing the opening double bracket `[[` to a single `[`, so the string it presents as R output is a string R never emits.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader trying to recognise this error cannot match the quoted text against what their console actually prints, and a web search for "Error en options[sprintf" returns nothing, so they will not identify the out.width/out.height chunk-option fix this section exists to give them.

heading: Package errors
proposition: The English names plyr::summarise() and stats::filter() as further sources of MASKING errors (namespace conflicts); the French calls them "erreurs de cache" (cache errors), a different mechanism the English does not mention.
reader_consequence: A French reader treats the plyr/stats conflicts as a caching problem rather than as the same namespace-masking problem described in the preceding sentence, so the link between the two paragraphs and the recommendation of the conflicted package loses its rationale, and the reader may look for a cache to clear instead of qualifying the call with dplyr::.

heading: Package errors / パッケージエラー
proposition: The English names `plyr::summarise()` as a common source of masking errors; the Japanese names `plyr::summary()` instead, a function plyr does not export.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader hunting a masking conflict searches for `plyr::summary()`, finds no such function, and fails to recognise that the real conflict is between `plyr::summarise()` and `dplyr::summarise()`. Every other translation (fr, es, pt, ru, tr, vn) keeps `summarise()`, so this is a Japanese-only defect.

heading: Plotting errors / プロットのエラー
proposition: The English says the manual scale VALUES supplied (two colours) are insufficient for the number of factor levels; the Japanese says the NUMBER OF FACTOR LEVELS is insufficient (因子型の水準の数が十分ではありません), reversing which side of the mismatch is short.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader tries to add factor levels to the data, when the fix is to add a third colour to `scale_fill_manual(values = ...)`. The error text itself ("3 needed but only 2 provided") then reads as contradicting the surrounding explanation.

heading: Plotting errors / プロットのエラー
proposition: The English warns to consider whether NA has BECOME an extra factor level (a cause of the shortfall); the Japanese asks the reader to check whether NA is CORRECTLY a factor level (NA が正しく因子型の水準になっているか), presenting NA-as-a-level as the desired state rather than the suspected problem.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader treats an NA level as something to establish rather than as the unnoticed extra level that made two colours too few, so they do not remove or recount it and the plot still fails.

heading: Common errors / よくあるエラー (chapter intro)
proposition: The Japanese adds a translator's note stating that R error messages are not all translated into Japanese, and that where a Japanese version exists it is shown after the English one. The English has no such statement.
reader_consequence: No harm to the reader: it correctly explains the paired English/Japanese code blocks that the translation adds throughout. Recorded because it is propositional content with no English counterpart, and because it governs how the rest of the chapter is read.

heading: Interpreting error messages / Interpretando mensagens de erro
proposition: The Portuguese text asserts that a reproducible example is also called an 'MRE', standing for 'Minimal Reproducible Exemple'; the English names only 'reprex'.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader learns a second acronym that the handbook never uses again and that the linked 'Getting help' page does not define, and is given it with a misspelled expansion ('Exemple' for 'Example'), so a forum search on that term may not match what the handbook covers.

heading: Miscellaneous / Diversos
proposition: The Portuguese text identifies the pipe as the specific operator '%>%'; the English says only 'pipe' without naming an operator.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader takes the advice as applying only to the magrittr pipe '%>%' and may not check the same mistake in code written with the native pipe '|>'.

heading: Package errors
proposition: English gives the remedy for the masked select(): write dplyr:: explicitly, or re-order package loading so that dplyr is loaded after all the others. The Turkish sentence folds both remedies into the agent of the masking clause ('masked by MASS::select(), by the one specifying dplyr:: or re-ordering your package for dplyr'), so no remedy is stated.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader learns that select() was masked but is never told what to do about it, and in particular never learns that dplyr must be loaded last.

heading: Factor errors
proposition: The comment line names the value being added to the factor. English names it "Missing", matching the replace_na(age_cat, "Missing") call shown two lines below. Turkish names it "Eksik", which appears nowhere in the code beside it.
reader_consequence: The reader cannot connect the described value to the replace_na() call in the same block, and may believe the string literal in the call is localised when it is not.

heading: Typo errors
proposition: The prose tells the reader which literal string to look for in the error. English says look for "unexpected symbol", which is exactly the text in the block above it. Turkish says look for "Beklenmeyen simge", a string R never emits and which does not appear in the block above it.
reader_consequence: The reader scans real R output for a Turkish phrase that never occurs, and does not recognise the English 'unexpected symbol' message as the one meant.

heading: Function syntax errors
proposition: The leading comment states the cause of the error. English: recode() was run WITHOUT re-stating the x variable inside mutate(x = recode(x, OLD = NEW)). Turkish turns it into an instruction: 'repeat the code in order to re-state the x variable in mutate(x = recode(x, OLD = NEW))'.
reader_consequence: The reader takes the comment as a fix to apply rather than as the mistake that produced the error, so the diagnosis of the following error message is lost.

heading: Factor errors
proposition: The comment describes an action already taken. English: 'Tried to add a value to a factor'. Turkish uses the imperative 'eklemeye çalışın' ('try to add a value to a factor'), an instruction to the reader.
reader_consequence: The reader reads the line as a step to perform instead of the mistake that generated the invalid-factor-level error below it.

heading: Factor errors
proposition: The line reproduces R's verbatim error output. English shows 'Problem with `mutate()` input `age_cat`.' Turkish replaces it with a Turkish sentence, "'age_cat' girişi 'mutate()' ile ilgili sorun olur.", presenting as R output text that R does not emit. The two lines below it in the same block remain in English.
reader_consequence: The reader does not recognise the real English error message when it appears in their console, and cannot search for it verbatim.

heading: R Markdown errors
proposition: English states a prohibition: use out.width= or out.height= and *not* fig.width= and fig.height=. The Turkish sentence stops at 'kontrol edin' and leaves the rest as a fragment in which the emphasised word 'not' is untranslated; in Turkish 'not' means 'note', so the prohibition is not conveyed.
reader_consequence: The reader may read the fragment as 'also note fig.width= and fig.height=' and keep using the very options that cause the error.

heading: Plotting errors
proposition: The illustrated scale_fill_manual() call uses R colour literals. English shows c("orange", "purple"). Turkish shows c("turuncu", "mor"), which are not R colour names and would raise an invalid colour name error.
reader_consequence: A reader copying the illustrated values gets an invalid-colour error instead of the insufficient-values error the section is about.

heading: Miscellaneous
proposition: English tells the reader to check the pipes (%>%) between re-arranged dplyr verbs. Turkish renders 'piped' as 'Tünellenmiş' ('tunnelled') and 'pipe' as 'tünel' ('tunnel'), so the text refers to a tunnel in the middle and a tunnel at the end, which the English does not support and which has no referent in R.
reader_consequence: The reader cannot tell that the advice is about a missing or leftover %>% operator, so the single check this section offers is unusable.

heading: Interpreting error messages
proposition: English links the Getting help page as [Getting help](help.qmd). Turkish writes [Yardım alma] with no link target, so the cross-reference to that chapter is absent.
reader_consequence: The reader is told to see a page on getting help but is given no way to reach it, and the text renders as literal brackets.

heading: Common errors
proposition: English links Noam Ross's analysis at .../blob/master/misc/stack-overflow-common-r-errors.md. In Turkish the URL is cut after '/misc' and the remaining path fragment '/stack-overflow-common-r-errors.md' is left in the running text, so the link does not point at the analysis.
reader_consequence: A reader following the link lands on a directory rather than the cited analysis of common R error messages.

heading: Resources
proposition: English links the r-bloggers post as a single markdown link. In Turkish the closing bracket and the opening parenthesis are separated by intervening words, so the markdown link is broken and the resource is not hyperlinked.
reader_consequence: The only resource in the chapter renders as bracketed text plus a bare URL, so the reader cannot click through to it.

heading: Package errors
proposition: English gives three causes for 'could not find function': a typo, forgetting to install the package, or forgetting to load it. Turkish gives a typo and a single 'yüklemeyi unuttuğunuz', collapsing install and load into one verb.
reader_consequence: A reader whose package is installed but not attached with library() is not pointed at the loading step as a separate cause.

heading: Package errors / Cac loi lien quan den Package
proposition: The English states the 00LOCK recovery procedure: open the R library folder in your computer directory (e.g. R/win-library/), find the folder named 00LOCK, delete it manually, retry the install, and understand that an interrupted previous install caused it. The Vietnamese sentence translates only the opening conditional clause and leaves the whole procedure and its cause in untranslated English.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese-only reader reaches the 00LOCK error, reads the translated condition, and then hits English text. They do not learn where the library folder is, that the 00LOCK folder must be deleted by hand, that the install must be retried, or that an interrupted install is the cause. They cannot recover from the error using this chapter.

heading: R Markdown errors / Loi R Markdown
proposition: The English qualifies the trigger as an error message that CONTAINS SOMETHING LIKE `Error in options[[sprintf("fig.%s", i)]]`; the Vietnamese states the error message IS that string ('Neu thong bao loi la'), dropping the approximate-match qualifier.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader whose error message merely resembles the quoted string, or embeds it in a longer message, concludes the advice does not apply and does not check their knitr out.width / out.height chunk options.

heading: Modify theme / Modificar el tema
proposition: The theme() reference table says plot.caption = element_text() adjusts the legend ("La leyenda"), whereas the English says it adjusts the caption.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looking for the argument that styles the plot legend picks plot.caption and changes the caption text instead; the same reader also loses the table's only pointer to the caption argument, because everywhere else in this chapter 'leyenda' denotes the ggplot legend and 'pie del gráfico' denotes the caption.

heading: Free or fixed axes / Ejes libres o fijos
proposition: The translation names the argument as `scale = "free"`, while the English names `scales = "free"` and the code chunk beside it uses `facet_wrap(~District, scales = "free")`.
reader_consequence: A reader who copies `scale = "free"` into facet_grid() gets an ignored/unknown argument, the axes stay fixed, and `space = "free_y"` silently has no effect.

heading: Scaled to column values / Escalado a los valores de la columna
proposition: The translation says the alternative is to plot objects with sizes proportional to their column values, restricting the mechanism to the size aesthetic; the English says any plot aesthetic can be scaled by the values in a column.
reader_consequence: A reader concludes that only size can be driven by a column, which contradicts the section's own first example (color mapped to age) and discourages mapping color, shape or alpha to data.

heading: Plot aesthetics / Estética del gráfico
proposition: The translation says `color =` sets the colour of the point's perimeter ("el color del perimetro del punto") when using geom_point(); the English says it sets the point colour.
reader_consequence: A reader expects color= to draw only an outline on points and reaches for fill= to colour the dot, which does nothing for the default point shape, so the points come out unchanged.

heading: Import data / Importar datos
proposition: The translation states that ct_blood holds the cycle-threshold value of the PCR test ("cycle threshold, umbral de ciclo del test de PCR"); the English says only "CT values".
reader_consequence: The Spanish reader is given an interpretation of the variable that the English text never asserts, so the two editions disagree on what ct_blood measures and the claim is not verifiable from the handbook itself.

heading: Resources / Recursos
proposition: The translation adds that the listed pages carry material in English ("Consulta las siguietnes páginas con maerial en inglés"); the English text makes no claim about the language of the resources.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader who avoids English-language material skips the whole list, even though two of the listed links point to the Spanish edition of R for Data Science (es.r4ds.hadley.nz), so the added claim is contradicted by the list beneath it.

heading: Box plots / Diagrammes en boites
proposition: The French text says the fill aesthetic is set to the column `gender`, glossed as "issue finale de chaque cas" (each case's final outcome); the English says the fill is set to the column `outcome`, and the column `gender` holds sex, not outcome.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told that the column `gender` contains each case's final outcome, so they will look for death/recovery values in the sex column and misread the legend of plot B, which is coloured by sex.

heading: Facets / Small-multiples
proposition: With two variables in `facet_wrap()`, the panel headings show combined terms and carry no separate row-versus-column logic.
reader_consequence: A French reader who passes two variables to `facet_wrap()` is not warned that the strip labels merge both terms, so they will expect row and column headings like `facet_grid()` produces and misread the resulting panel labels.

heading: Mapping data to the plot / "Mappage"
proposition: The French text adds that the automatically generated y-axis of `geom_histogram()` represents the count of each "modalite" (each category/level of the variable); the English says only that the counts y-axis is generated automatically, and the histogram counts rows per bin of a continuous variable, not per category.
reader_consequence: A French reader learns that a histogram counts distinct values of a variable, which is the behaviour of `geom_bar()`, and so misses the bin-based nature of `geom_histogram()` that the chapter later insists on.

heading: Complete themes / Fonctions theme toute faites
proposition: The French note states that micro-adjustments made with `theme()` before a complete theme will not be taken into account ("sinon les ajustements ne seront pas pris en compte"); the English only says such adjustments should be made after the complete theme, without stating the consequence.
reader_consequence: A French reader receives an extra causal claim about override behaviour that the English original does not make, so the two editions teach a different rule about what happens when the order is reversed.

heading: ### General cleaning
proposition: The cross-reference for cleaning 'data friendly' underscore values into normal text or title case points to the Characters and strings chapter in English, but the translation points to the Cleaning data and core functions chapter (#cleaning).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader following the pointer lands on the data-cleaning chapter, which does not cover string case conversion, and never reaches the Characters and strings chapter where str_to_title() and friends are taught. The same #cleaning link is already given two paragraphs earlier, so the pointer is also a dead duplicate.

heading: ### Pivoting longer
proposition: English says the pivoted data has one ROW per possible symptom for each case; the translation says each case has 5 rows and then that there is one COLUMN per symptom.
reader_consequence: The whole point of pivot_longer() here is that symptoms stop being columns and become rows. A reader told there is one column per symptom in the long table misreads the output of the pivot, and cannot tell long format from the wide format shown just above.

heading: ### Plot aesthetics
proposition: The example of mapping an aesthetic to a data column is written color = hospital (bare column name) in English and color = "hospital" (quoted string) in the translation.
reader_consequence: A quoted value is a static assignment, the exact opposite of the mapping this bullet defines, and the chapter later states explicitly that the column name must not be in quotes. A reader copying aes(color = "hospital") gets every point drawn in one constant colour with a spurious one-item legend, not a grouping by hospital.

heading: ### Free or fixed axes
proposition: English states that faceted axis scales are by default the SAME (fixed) across all facets; the translation replaces that statement with a repeat of the following clause ('not always appropriate') and never says the default is fixed scales.
reader_consequence: The section exists to explain when to override the default with scales = "free". A reader who is never told the default is a shared fixed scale cannot see what scales = "free_y" changes, and may not realise that counts in different facets are directly comparable unless freed.

heading: ### `geom_col()`
proposition: The prose names the summary dataset built in the adjacent chunk as `outcomes` in English and as `outcome` in the translation.
reader_consequence: `outcome` is also the name of a real column in that table and in the linelist, so the reader cannot tell whether the text refers to the data frame or the column, and ggplot(outcome) fails because no such object exists.

heading: Rótulos / Labels
proposition: The translation says str_glue() was used in the TITLE assignment; the English says it was used in the CAPTION assignment, and the chunk beside it uses str_glue() only inside caption = .
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader looks for str_glue() in the title = argument of the labs() call above, where it does not appear, and may copy the dynamic-date pattern into title = instead of caption = .

heading: Modifique o tema / Modify theme
proposition: The translation attributes element_text(hjust = 0) to the plot TITLE; the English attributes it to the CAPTION, and the chunk beside it applies hjust = 0 to plot.caption, not to plot.title.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader believes hjust = 0 in the example controls the title and writes plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0) when trying to left-align a caption, producing the wrong element.

heading: `ggplot()`
proposition: The translation names the ggplot() dataset argument `dados = `; the English names it `data = `, and the chunk beside it writes ggplot(data = linelist).
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader who types ggplot(dados = linelist) gets an unused-argument error, because ggplot2 has no argument named dados.

heading: Modifique o tema / Modify theme
proposition: The translation describes the `axis.text = element_text()` table row as adjusting x-axis text; the English describes it as adjusting axis text on both axes.
reader_consequence: The axis.text row and the axis.text.x row now carry the identical description in Portuguese, so a reader cannot tell the two arguments apart and may use axis.text.x when both axes need the change.

heading: Fazer gráficos de dados contínuos / Plot continuous data
proposition: The translation adds a translator's note explaining that 'jitter' means agitated or nervous in English and that the points are spread so they do not overlap; the English has no such note.
reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader meets an in-text editorial aside in the bullet list of plot types that no other language edition carries; the content is correct but it is not part of the handbook text.

heading: ### Modify theme / ### Изменение темы
proposition: The Russian text states that `legend.position =` accepts the values "низ", "верх", "лево" and "право"; the English states it accepts "bottom", "top", "left" and "right", which are the only strings ggplot2 accepts.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who types `legend.position = "низ"` gets an error, and cannot tell from the text what the accepted strings actually are; the adjacent chunk at line 679 uses "bottom".

heading: ## Facets / Small-multiples / ## Фасеты/малые множества
proposition: The Russian text says `facet_grid()` takes "one or two ROWS" (одну или две строки) in the formula; the English says one or two COLUMNS (column names) are supplied to the formula.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader is told the formula names rows rather than data columns, which contradicts the very next clause of the same bullet ('only one column') and the `rows ~ columns` grid convention being explained.

heading: ### Set to a static value / ### Установить статистическое значение
proposition: The Russian heading says 'Set a STATISTICAL value' (статистическое); the English says 'Set to a STATIC value', and the section is about static (constant) aesthetic values.
reader_consequence: A reader scanning headings looks for the static-value rule under a heading that promises statistics, and the heading contradicts its own first sentence (line 245), which correctly says статичной.

heading: ## Plot continuous data / ## Построение графика непрерывных данных
proposition: In the English list, box plot, jitter plot, violin plot and sina plot are nested as sub-items of 'Plots for one continuous variable'; in the Russian list only the histogram stays nested, so those four are presented at the same level as the scatter plot (two variables) and heat plot (three variables).
reader_consequence: A Russian reader does not learn that box, jitter, violin and sina plots belong to the one-continuous-variable family, and may read them as an unrelated category alongside two- and three-variable plots.

heading: ## Basics of ggplot / ## Основы ggplot
proposition: The English lists four example geometries: bar graph, line plot, scatter plot, histogram. The Russian renders both 'bar graph' and 'histogram' as 'гистограмма', so the bar graph example is absent and 'гистограмма' appears twice.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader loses the bar graph as an example geometry and sees a list that names the same shape twice, in a chapter that later insists bar charts and histograms are distinct (lines 781, 1161).

heading: ### Histograms / ### Гистограммы
proposition: The verbatim console output block is translated into Russian ('## `stat_bin()`, используя `bins = 30`. Подберите лучшее значение...'), asserting that R prints this message in Russian; R prints the English string shown in the original.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader will not match the quoted text to the message R actually prints, and cannot search for it verbatim when troubleshooting.

heading: ### Scaled to column values / ### Масштабирование по значениям столбца
proposition: The Russian text names the mapped aesthetic as `Size = ` with a capital S; the English and the adjacent chunk (line 292 EN / 292 TR) use the lower-case `size = `, which is the only spelling R accepts.
reader_consequence: A reader copying `Size = age` into `aes()` gets an unknown-aesthetic result rather than a scaled point size.

heading: Geoms
proposition: The English says ggplot2 itself contains over 40 geoms and that many FURTHER geoms are created by fans; the Turkish says the 40-plus geoms in ggplot2 were created by volunteers/fans, and drops the existence of additional community geoms.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader believes ggplot2's built-in geoms are community contributions, and does not learn that a large extra set of geoms exists outside the package, so they will not look for extension geoms at the linked gallery.

heading: Groups
proposition: The English states that using only group = inside aes() will NOT create a legend; the Turkish states that it WILL also create a new legend.
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who wants a legend uses group = alone, gets no legend, and cannot tell whether the plot or their code is wrong.

heading: Modify theme
proposition: The English lists the literal values legend.position accepts as "bottom", "top", "left" and "right"; the Turkish lists them as "alt", "üst", "sol" and "sağ", which ggplot2 does not accept and which the adjacent chunk contradicts (it uses legend.position = "bottom").
reader_consequence: The reader writes legend.position = "alt" and the plot fails or ignores the setting, with no hint in the text that the value must stay in English.

heading: Histograms
proposition: The English instructs the reader to set y = after_stat(density); the Turkish writes y = after_stat(yoğunluk), while the code chunk immediately below (tr 807, 812) uses after_stat(density).
reader_consequence: The reader copies after_stat(yoğunluk) and gets an error, because no such statistic exists; the same line tells them to use the syntax exactly, so they have no reason to suspect the translated word.

heading: Labels
proposition: The English says the caption shows the maximum hospitalisation DATE in the linelist; the Turkish says it shows the maximum hospital stay DURATION, which the adjacent code (max(linelist$date_hospitalisation)) contradicts.
reader_consequence: The reader misreads the caption of their own plot as a length of stay rather than a data cut-off date, and may reuse the str_glue() pattern believing it computes a duration.

heading: ggplot basics (introduction)
proposition: The English says tidyverse-compatible formatting makes using ggplot2 and the tidyverse packages together very EFFECTIVE; the Turkish says it makes using many packages together OBLIGATORY ("zorunlu kılar").
reader_consequence: The reader concludes ggplot2 cannot be used without adopting a set of other packages, which may deter them from using ggplot2 with base data structures.

heading: Free or fixed axes
proposition: The English gives "free" as the literal value to release both axes; the Turkish, in the same list as "free_x", tells the reader to write "serbest", which ggplot2 does not accept and which the adjacent chunk (scales = "free", tr 472) contradicts.
reader_consequence: The reader writes scales = "serbest" to free both axes and the call fails, while the two neighbouring values ("free_y", "free_x") work, giving no clue why.

heading: Box plots
proposition: The English says geom_boxplot() creates a BOX plot; the Turkish body text says geom_boxplot() creates a bar chart ("çubuk grafiği"), the same term the chapter uses elsewhere for geom_bar()/geom_col() (tr 175, tr 985 onward).
reader_consequence: The reader conflates box plots with bar charts, and within the same paragraph meets both "çubuk grafiği" and "kutu grafiği" for the same object, so they cannot tell which geom produces which figure.

heading: Facets / Small-multiples
proposition: The English says the quick faceting examples that follow use the malaria dataset, with a parenthetical link to the download page; the Turkish says to look at the "Download handbook and data" page FOR those examples.
reader_consequence: The reader leaves the chapter to find worked examples on the download page, which holds only data-download instructions, and may miss that the examples are in the next few sections.

heading: Histograms
proposition: The English shows the stat_bin() console message in a plain fenced block, as the console output the prose promises; the Turkish wraps the same text in an executable R chunk carrying figure options (```{r fig.show='hold', out.width=c('50%','50%')}), so it renders as R source rather than as the message.
reader_consequence: The reader is told a message appears after the plot, then sees what looks like a runnable code chunk containing only a comment, so they may try to run it or take the message for code they must type.

heading: facet_wrap()
proposition: The English says one facet is created for EACH unique value of District; the translation says "chỉ một facet được tạo ra cho giá trị duy nhất của cột District" (only one facet is created for the unique value of the District column), asserting a single facet rather than one per district.
reader_consequence: A Vietnamese reader expects facet_wrap(~District) to produce a single panel, so the multi-panel figure the chunk actually renders contradicts the text and the core purpose of faceting (one panel per group) is lost.

heading: Import data
proposition: The translation states the chapter focuses on TWO continuous variables ("tập trung [vào] hai biến liên tục") and then lists four (age, wt_kg, ct_blood, days_onset_hosp); the English states "the continuous variables" and gives no count.
reader_consequence: The stated count contradicts the list beside it, so a reader cannot tell which two of the four columns the chapter will use and may skip two of the variables that later examples rely on.

heading: Modify theme
proposition: For element_text(hjust = 0) the English gives the direction as "(from right to left)"; the translation gives the opposite direction, "(từ trái qua phải)" (from left to right).
reader_consequence: A reader taking the parenthetical as the direction of the hjust scale infers the reversed convention and sets hjust to the wrong end when aligning a caption or title.

heading: Colorbrewer and Viridis / Colorbrewer y Viridis
proposition: The English says the viridis palettes are colourblind friendly; the Spanish says they are '¡difíciles para los daltónicos!' (difficult for the colourblind), the opposite claim.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader concludes viridis is a bad choice for colourblind audiences and avoids scale_xxx_viridis_*, choosing exactly the palettes the chapter warns against, even though the quotation in the same sentence says viridis is designed to be perceived by viewers with common forms of colour blindness.

heading: Time axes / Ejes temporales
proposition: The English recommends assigning labels = scales::label_date_short() inside scale_x_date() to build efficient date labels that adjust automatically as the data span grows from days to weeks to months to years, and points to the Epicurves multi-level date labels section; the Spanish section ends before this and never mentions label_date_short().
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader never learns the automatic date-label solution and keeps hand-tuning date_breaks and date_labels, producing crowded or stale axis labels as the epicurve time span grows.

heading: Time axes / Ejes temporales
proposition: The English Time axes section contains a second runnable code chunk demonstrating scale_x_date(labels = scales::label_date_short()); the Spanish section has no counterpart chunk and ends after the first example.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader has no worked example to copy for the label_date_short() approach, so the rendered Spanish page shows one date-axis figure where the English shows two.

heading: Scales for color, fill, axes, etc.
proposition: The translation states that point size can be adjusted according to the minimum and maximum values using `scale_size`, and colour tied to a given variable modified with `scale_color`; the English gives no such per-aesthetic examples and never mentions `scale_size` or min/max-based sizing.
reader_consequence: A French reader is told `scale_size` rescales by the data minimum and maximum, an argument-level behaviour the chapter never demonstrates or documents, and may look for min/max options that the section does not cover.

heading: Continuous axes scales
proposition: The translation says the `c()` vector supplied to `breaks = ` contains the NUMBER of desired graduations ("le nombre de graduation souhaitées"); the English says it contains the desired break VALUES.
reader_consequence: A French reader may write `breaks = c(10)` expecting ten evenly spaced ticks and instead get a single break at the value 10, then conclude the argument does not work.

heading: Colorbrewer and Viridis
proposition: The translation lists the third viridis scale variant as "binaire" (binary); the English says "binned", which is the `scale_*_viridis_b` binned-scale variant.
reader_consequence: A French reader looks for a two-value binary palette that does not exist, and misses that ggplot2 offers a binned viridis scale (`scale_fill_viridis_b`) for grouping a continuous variable into intervals.

heading: Contour lines
proposition: The translation adds the sentence "Elles permettent une différente visualisation de la répartition des points dans l'espace" (contour lines give a different visualisation of how the points are distributed in space); the English paragraph makes no such claim.
reader_consequence: A French reader is given an extra, unsourced rationale for contour plots that the English chapter does not state and that no figure in the section demonstrates.

heading: Combine legends
proposition: The translation says to remove one plot's legend "pour éviter la dé-duplication" (to AVOID de-duplication); the English says removing it IS the de-duplication.
reader_consequence: A French reader reads the stated purpose of the step as the opposite of what it is, and may leave both legends in place believing removal is what should be avoided.

heading: Point-and-click ggplot2 with esquisse
proposition: The translation opens with "**equisse** fournit une interface graphique pour la construction de graphiques avec **ggplot2**", a descriptive claim about the package that the English section does not make; the English gives only the quoted addin description.
reader_consequence: Low impact, but the French reader receives an editorial description presented alongside the quoted vendor text, blurring which words are the quotation.

heading: Resources
proposition: The English attributes the surveillance-data presentation guidelines to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control; the translation drops the ECDC attribution and gives the bare link.
reader_consequence: A French reader cannot tell who publishes the guidelines, so cannot judge their authority or cite them, and must open the PDF to find the issuing body.

heading: Gradient scales / 勾配スケール
proposition: The English attributes the multi-colour vector argument to `scale_fill_gradientn()`; the Japanese names `scale_fill_gradient()` again, which is not the function used in the code chunk below (jp lines 345-349 call `scale_fill_gradientn()`).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader sees the same function name in both bullets, cannot tell the two-colour function from the n-colour function, and will call `scale_fill_gradient()` with a colour vector, which errors or ignores the extra colours.

heading: Time axes / 時間スケール
proposition: The Japanese second sentence names the function `label_date_sort()`; the English names `label_date_short()` throughout, and the code chunk below (jp line 663) calls `scales::label_date_short()`.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader who copies the name from the prose calls a function that does not exist in the scales package and gets 'could not find function' instead of short date labels.

heading: Plotting multiple datasets / 複数のデータセットをプロットする
proposition: The English strategy is to merge the data AND convert it to 'long' format before plotting; the Japanese keeps only the merge plus adding a dataset-identifying column, and omits the conversion to long format.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader merges the datasets wide, has no single value column to map to an aesthetic, and cannot reproduce the recommended one-plot-from-several-datasets approach.

heading: Time axes / 時間スケール
proposition: The Japanese states that the Epidemic curves section sits inside the preceding ggplot basics chapter ('前章 ggplotの基礎 内 流行曲線 の章'); the English points to the separate Epidemic curves page and its ggplot section, and never places Epidemic curves inside ggplot basics.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader looks for date-axis examples inside the ggplot basics chapter, does not find them, and misses the Epidemic curves chapter that actually holds them.

heading: Smart Labeling / スマートラベリング
proposition: The English says there is no ideal way to solve label clashes in the base package (base ggplot2), for which ggrepel is the add-on; the Japanese says the problem is hard to solve with R's base functions ('R の base 関数').
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader attributes the label-collision limitation to base R graphics rather than to ggplot2 itself, and may assume plain ggplot2 geom_text()/geom_label() already handles overlap.

heading: Time axes / Eixos de tempo
proposition: Assigning `labels = scales::label_date_short()` inside `scale_x_date()` builds efficient x-axis date labels automatically.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader never learns the `label_date_short()` technique and also loses its worked ggplot example, so they keep hand-specifying `date_breaks` and `date_labels` for every plot.

heading: Time axes / Eixos de tempo
proposition: The labels produced by `label_date_short()` adjust themselves automatically as the data extend over time, from days to weeks to months to years.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader does not know that this label approach survives a growing time series, so they do not consider it for a surveillance plot that is re-rendered as the outbreak lengthens.

heading: Time axes / Eixos de tempo
proposition: A complete example of multi-level date labels is available in the Epidemic curves page.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader loses the cross-reference and cannot find the full worked example of multi-level date labels elsewhere in the handbook.

heading: Gradient scales / Escalas em gradiente
proposition: The translation states that the code produces a "raster" FILE ("produzimos um arquivo 'raster' de um gráfico de densidade de calor"); the English states that the plot itself is a raster heat-tile density plot, and the chunk beside it only sets `geom = "raster"` inside `stat_density2d()` and writes nothing to disk.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader expects the chunk to write a raster image file, looks for an output file that never appears, and misreads `geom = "raster"` as an export format rather than as the ggplot2 geom that draws the tiles.

heading: Scales / Escalas
proposition: The translation states that other CLASSES exist ("Existem outras classes"); the English states that other METHOD suffixes exist beyond `_discrete()`, `continuous()`, `_date()`, `_gradient()` and `_manual()`.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese reader takes the sentence as a remark about extra column classes rather than about extra scale-method suffixes, so they do not go looking for further `scale_AESTHETIC_METHOD()` variants such as `_binned()`.

heading: Smart Labeling
proposition: English says to include `fill = ` WITHIN `aes()` to colour the label by value; the Russian says to use `fill = ` OUTSIDE of `aes()`.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader places `fill = outcome` outside `aes()` in `geom_label_repel()`, which errors on an unknown object or produces a single static fill, so labels are never coloured by outcome. The very next code chunk (line 611) puts `fill = outcome` inside `aes()`, contradicting the instruction.

heading: Marginal distributions
proposition: English lists the literal allowed values of `type = ` as "histogram", "density", "boxplot", "violin", "densigram"; the Russian replaces those literal strings with Russian words ("гистограмма", "плотность", "коробчатая диаграмма", "скрипичная диаграмма", "денсиграмма").
reader_consequence: A Russian reader writes `type = "гистограмма"` and `ggMarginal()` fails, because the argument only accepts the English enum. The adjacent chunks at lines 514 and 541 use `type = "histogram"` and `type = "boxplot"`, so the prose contradicts the code it introduces.

heading: Time axes
proposition: English gives the `date_breaks` examples as the literal strings `"3 months"` and `"2 days"`; the Russian gives them as `"3 месяца"` and `"2 дня"`.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader passes `date_breaks = "3 месяца"` to `scale_x_date()` and the call fails, because the interval string must be English. The chunk directly below (line 647) uses `date_breaks = "1 months"`.

heading: Scale arguments
proposition: English says `labels = ` controls HOW the values display; the Russian says `labels = ` controls the ORDER of display of the values ("порядок отображения значений").
reader_consequence: A Russian reader believes `labels = ` reorders discrete levels and tries to reorder categories by rearranging the label vector. `labels = ` only renames levels in place, so the labels are silently attached to the wrong bars, producing a mislabelled plot with no error.

heading: Dual axes
proposition: English lists the literal `align = ` options as "hv", "h", "v", "none"; the Russian renders the fourth option as "без выравнивания" instead of the literal "none".
reader_consequence: A Russian reader who wants no alignment passes `align = "без выравнивания"` to `cowplot::align_plots()` and the call fails, because only the English literal "none" is accepted.

heading: Marginal distributions
proposition: English names the argument `size = `; the Russian capitalises it as `Size = `.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader copies `Size = ` into `ggMarginal()`. R argument matching is case-sensitive, so the argument is not recognised and the call errors or the size is silently ignored. The English text at line 534, translated correctly as `size = `, then disagrees with this bullet.

heading: Time axes / Zaman eksenleri
proposition: Assigning `labels = scales::label_date_short()` inside `scale_x_date()` builds efficient x-axis date labels automatically, and those labels adjust themselves as the data span grows from days to weeks to months to years.
reader_consequence: The Turkish reader never learns the `label_date_short()` shortcut, loses the runnable example chunk that demonstrates it, and loses the pointer to the Epicurves 'multi-level date labels' section. They are left only with manual `date_breaks`/`date_labels` and will hand-tune axis labels every time the date range changes.

heading: Color schemes / Renk şemaları
proposition: Inside `aes()` the aesthetic is mapped with `color = hospital`, and outside `aes()` a static value is set with `color = "blue"`.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text writes these as `renk = hastane` and `color= "mavi"`. Neither exists: `linelist` has no `hastane` column and `"mavi"` is not an R colour name, while the chunk directly below uses `color = "purple"` and `aes(color = gender)`. A reader copying the prose gets 'object not found' or 'invalid color name' errors.

heading: Continuous axes scales / Sürekli eksen ölçekleri
proposition: The argument that supplies the sequence of axis break values is named `breaks = `.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text instructs the reader to use a `kesmeler = ` argument, which does not exist in ggplot2, while the chunk immediately below uses `breaks = seq(...)`. A reader following the prose gets an 'unused argument' error from `scale_y_continuous()`.

heading: Dual axes / Çift eksen
proposition: The two plots are made to share an x-axis by giving both the same `date_breaks` and `date_labels` arguments.
reader_consequence: The Turkish bullet names these arguments `tarih_araları` and `tarih_etiketleri`, which do not exist, while the p1 and p2 chunks below both use `date_breaks = "month"` and `date_labels = "%b"`. A reader cannot find the named arguments and may not realise the two axes must be configured identically.

heading: Color schemes / Renk şemaları
proposition: Exterior colour of a plot object is controlled by the aesthetic named `color = ` and interior colour by the aesthetic named `fill = `.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text names them `renk = ` and `dolgu = `, which are not ggplot2 aesthetics, while the chunk below uses `color = "red"` and `fill = "lightblue"`. The reader learns the wrong argument names for the single most-used pair of aesthetics in the chapter.

heading: Gradient scales / Gradyan ölçekleri
proposition: `scale_fill_gradientn()` takes the colour vector through an argument written `values = `.
reader_consequence: The Turkish bullet writes the argument as "değerler =", which does not exist, while the chunk below uses `colors = c(...)` and `values = scales::rescale(...)`. The reader cannot match the bullet to any argument in the example code.

heading: Scales / Ölçekler
proposition: The first part of a scale function name, `scale_`, is invariant: it never changes.
reader_consequence: The Turkish text reads 'İlk kısım olan `scale_()` düzeltildi' ('the first part, `scale_()`, was corrected/repaired'), which states an edit was made rather than that the prefix is fixed. The reader loses the rule that only the second and third parts of `scale_AESTHETIC_METHOD()` vary, which is the point of the three-part list.

heading: Combine legends / Göstergeleri birleştir
proposition: Removing the legend from one of two plots that share the same legend de-duplicates the legend.
reader_consequence: The Turkish parenthetical says '(tekrarlanacaktır)' ('it will be repeated'), asserting the opposite outcome of the instruction it annotates. A reader may conclude that deleting one legend produces a duplicated legend and skip the step, ending up with two identical legends in the combined figure.

heading: Color schemes / Renk şemaları
proposition: The complete list of R colour names is at http://sape.inf.usi.ch/quick-reference/ggplot2/colour.
reader_consequence: The Turkish link target was respelled to .../ggplot2/color, a path that does not exist on that site. A reader clicking 'tam liste' reaches a dead page instead of the colour-name reference.

heading: Resources / Kaynaklar
proposition: The ggplot2 cheatsheet is at http://zevross.com/blog/2014/08/04/beautiful-plotting-in-r-a-ggplot2-cheatsheet-3/.
reader_consequence: The Turkish link target was respelled to .../beauty-plotting-in-r-a-ggplot2-cheatsheet-3/, which does not resolve. The reader cannot reach the cheatsheet from the Resources list, even though the correct URL still appears in a commented-out block later in the same file.

heading: Time axes / Trục thời gian
proposition: Assigning `labels = scales::label_date_short()` inside `scale_x_date()` builds efficient x-axis date labels automatically, and those labels re-adjust on their own as the data span grows from days to weeks to months to years.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader finishes the Time axes section knowing only the manual `date_breaks` / `date_labels` route, never learns the `label_date_short()` shortcut, and loses the accompanying runnable example chunk that the English chapter provides, so they hand-tune date label formats that would otherwise adapt by themselves.

heading: Time axes / Trục thời gian
proposition: A complete worked example of efficient date labels exists in the Epicurves page, in its section on multi-level date labels.
reader_consequence: The Vietnamese reader gets no pointer to the fuller treatment of multi-level date labels elsewhere in the handbook, so they cannot follow up when the brief in-page guidance is not enough.

heading: Github issues / Issues en Github
proposition: The English sentence carries a working cross-reference to the Collaboration and Github chapter, written as a markdown link [Collaboration and Github](collaboration.qmd); the Spanish writes [Colaboración y Github]{#version-control-and-collaboration-with-git-and-github}, which is span-attribute syntax, not link syntax, so no cross-reference exists in the translation.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader is told to read more about storing work on Github 'on the page Colaboración y Github', but the text renders as plain unlinked words. The reader cannot reach the chapter and has no file name or URL to find it by.

heading: The reprex package / El paquete reprex
proposition: The English says the arguments and possible variations are documented in the reprex documentation (a separate resource, given as a link labelled 'documentation'); the Spanish says they can be read 'en esta página' ('on this page'), locating that material inside the handbook page itself.
reader_consequence: A Spanish reader looks for a fuller account of the reprex arguments on the current handbook page, where it does not exist, instead of going to the reprex package documentation. The reader may conclude the page is incomplete rather than consulting the external reference.

heading: The **reprex** package / Le package **reprex**
proposition: The English says the reprex HTML output contains any warnings produced by the code; the French replaces "warnings" with "messages", so the claim that warnings are captured is absent.
reader_consequence: A French reader may not expect warnings to appear in the reprex output, and may separately paste warning text into a forum post believing reprex did not capture it. In R, message() and warning() are distinct conditions, so the substituted term names a different output type.

heading: The **reprex** package / **reprex** パッケージとは？
proposition: The English says the `wd =` argument is where you SUPPLY a working directory to reprex; the Japanese says that using `wd =` lets you DISPLAY the working directory (作業ディレクトリを表示できます).
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader believes `wd =` is a flag that prints the working directory into the reprex output, so they will not pass a directory path to it and will not know how to point reprex at a different project folder.

heading: The **reprex** package / **reprex** パッケージとは？
proposition: The English says that because **reprex** ships with **tidyverse** you may load EITHER package; the Japanese instructs the reader to load **tidyverse** only.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader does not learn that loading **reprex** alone is sufficient, so they load the whole tidyverse when only the one package is needed.

heading: Minimal data / 最小限のデータとは？
proposition: The English offers anonymising and subsetting as options to CONSIDER; the Japanese states they are NECESSARY (必要になります) to build a minimal dataset.
reader_consequence: A Japanese reader treats anonymisation and subsetting as mandatory steps for every minimal dataset, rather than as suggestions to weigh against their own data.

heading: Posting to a forum / Postar em um fórum
proposition: The reproducible example posted to a forum should include your R session information.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese bullet reads 'com as informações do seu trabalho' (information about your work), so a reader omits R and package version output (sessionInfo / session_info) from the forum post, and answerers cannot reproduce version-dependent behaviour.

heading: The **reprex** package / O pacote **reprex**
proposition: Setting session_info = TRUE causes the output of sessioninfo::session_info() to be included in the reprex output.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese sentence only says session_info() output 'will include your R and package versions'; it never states that the argument adds that output to the reprex. A reader does not learn what the argument actually changes in the posted reprex.

heading: The **reprex** package / O pacote **reprex**
proposition: Typing `?Reprex` opens the reprex documentation.
reader_consequence: R help lookup is case sensitive, so `?Reprex` returns 'No documentation for Reprex'. The English gives `?reprex`, which works. A Portuguese reader following the text fails to open the help page.

heading: Getting help / Conseguindo ajuda
proposition: A reproducible example is also called an MRE, for 'Minimal reproducible example'.
reader_consequence: The Portuguese introduces an acronym (MRE) and an expansion that the English chapter never uses again, so a reader may search the handbook for a term it does not contain.

heading: Posting to a forum
proposition: The English names two independent resources to read (the Stack Overflow 'how to ask a good question' guide, and the Stack Overflow code of conduct); the Russian joins them with the preposition 'в', asserting that the good-question posts are located inside the code of conduct.
reader_consequence: A Russian reader treats the code of conduct as the container of the how-to-ask guidance rather than as a second document worth reading on its own, so they may skip the code of conduct entirely once they have opened the first link.

heading: ### The **reprex** package
proposition: The English says reprex ships with tidyverse so loading EITHER package suffices; the Turkish says you must load BOTH packages ("her iki paketi de yüklemelisiniz").
reader_consequence: A Turkish reader believes a separate library(reprex) call is mandatory alongside tidyverse, and may conclude their setup is broken when the code chunk below loads only tidyverse.

proposition: The English link points the reader to the Collaboration and Github chapter at target collaboration.qmd; the Turkish keeps the label but drops the link target entirely, leaving bare text [İşbirliği ve Github].

heading: ## Resources
proposition: The English URL fragment is #producing-a-minimal-dataset; the Turkish URL fragment is #production-a-minimal-dataset, an anchor that does not exist on the target page.

proposition: The English provides a working markdown link whose label "get help!" is attached to the tidyverse help URL; in the Turkish the label [yardım alacağınız] is separated from the URL by the words "hakkında Tidyverse sayfası!", so no hyperlink is produced.
